content.text:
Both changes are in, tested and pushed (`c9f9bb9`).

**1. Local times in query output.** Every time in `search` results (`started_at`, `ended_at`) and the echoed window in both commands (`from`, `to`, `at`) is now in your local zone, with the offset:
```
"started_at": "2026-11-17T00:04:38.044+02:00"
```
That's still standard RFC 3339, so it stays unambiguous. The log and the database keep storing UTC.

**2. `text` reports the full app id.**
```
$ brain query text --app kons --from -3s
{ "app": "org.kde.konsole", ... }
```
- The candidates are the apps that have sessions, plus any app with keys or pastes in the requested window. Events that aren't typing, like the `start` event, don't count.
- An exact match wins, ignoring case. So `--app code` means `code` even though `com.microsoft.VSCode` also contains "code".
- Otherwise the one id that contains your text wins.
- **If several match, it's an error** listing them, so `text` never mixes two apps into one stream:
  `brain: error: "o" matches several apps: org.kde.konsole, synthetic; be more specific`
- **If none match, it's also an error**, listing the known apps. Before, it quietly returned empty text.
- A known app that had no typing in the window still returns empty text, with its full id.
- `search --app` is unchanged: it keeps every matching app, and each result already shows its full id.

**Tests:** new unit tests for the name resolution (exact over partial, several matches, none) and for local-time formatting. The CLI tests now check local times, full ids, and both error cases. Everything passes: 121 unit tests, crash safety, `query_cli`, `perf_budget`. The README and PLAN.md describe the new behavior.

No database change this time, so `! make` is all you need to use it.

**Notes on the rows that were close calls:**

- **evdev (A) vs libinput (B).** Both read the same device nodes. libinput's
  value is pointer acceleration, touchpad gestures and tablet handling, none of
  which we need. For keys it adds nothing over `struct input_event`. Reading
  evdev directly keeps the dependency set and the memory footprint small, and
  gives full control over hotplug and resync.
- **Why not grab (D).** A passive reader is *not on the input path*: the kernel
  delivers each event to every open evdev client independently. If brain
  stalls, the user notices nothing. A grab-and-forward proxy makes every
  keystroke wait on brain, needs root for `/dev/uinput`, and its failure mode
  (frozen keyboard) is the worst one possible. It only makes sense for tools
  that *modify* input (remappers); we only observe.
- **AT-SPI (F)** is the only system-wide source that sees real text rather than
  keys, and it is tempting for exactly that reason. In practice, coverage
  decides: our three target app classes (Chrome/Electron, VS Code, terminals)
  are the weak spots. It needs browser flags and a11y forced on, and terminal
  emulators expose little of their contents. It stays a future enhancement, as
  a *second source* that could correct key-based reconstruction for GTK/Qt
  apps. It would not replace evdev.
- **Compositor hook (H)** has the best key-level fidelity, but a plugin
  compiled against one KWin version and loaded into the user's compositor is a
  bad trade for a home-assignment tool: an ABI mismatch or a bug takes down the
  desktop. We take the one thing we need from the compositor (focus) through
  its *supported* scripting interface, and copy its keymap and repeat settings
  instead of hooking it.

content.content:
## Supported OS

Ubuntu (tested on 26.04) with **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Key capture
works on any Linux. Focus tracking needs KWin (Wayland or X11). On other
desktops, keys are recorded under the app `unknown`.

## Build

```sh
# Rust toolchain (https://rustup.rs), then:
cargo build --release
# binary: target/release/brain

# or build and install to /usr/bin/brain (asks for sudo for the copy only):
make
```

SQLite is bundled. libxkbcommon is loaded from the runtime library
`libxkbcommon.so.0` that every Wayland desktop ships, so no `-dev`
packages are needed.

## Permissions

`brain` reads keyboards directly from `/dev/input/event*` (read-only,
never grabbed, so it cannot add input lag). Your user must be in the `input`
group:

```sh
sudo usermod -aG input "$USER"   # then log out and back in
```

Note that the `input` group can read every input device. That is the price of
display-server-independent capture (see PLAN.md for the alternatives).

## Run

```sh
target/release/brain run --data-dir ~/brain-data
```

`run` stops cleanly on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. A `kill -9` is also safe. The next
start repairs a torn last line, if there is one, and resumes ingest exactly
where it stopped.

### As a service

`brain` can run as a **systemd user service**: it starts with your Plasma
session, restarts if it crashes, stops at logout, and runs as you (no
root; it needs your desktop session for focus tracking):

```sh
make install-service          # installs /usr/bin/brain + the unit, enables it
journalctl --user -u brain -f # its messages
systemctl --user stop brain   # pause capture
make uninstall-service        # remove it
```

The service uses `~/brain-data`. Stop it before running `brain run` by hand
on the same directory (only one `brain run` per data directory).

Add `--vscode-replay` to reconstruct VS Code sessions in a sandboxed,
invisible copy of VS Code (tier 2, below). It is off by default.

Data directory (mode 0700):

| File           | What                                                   |
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `events.jsonl` | append-only capture log, the ground truth              |
| `brain.db`     | SQLite (WAL) index derived from the log                |
| `run.lock`     | held by the running `brain run` (one per data dir)     |
| `kwin/`        | generated KWin focus-tracking script                   |
| `vscode/`      | VS Code replay sandbox and file snapshots (tier 2 only) |

Example log lines:

```json
{"ts":"2026-11-15T17:20:01.112Z","app":"org.kde.konsole","type":"focus","window":"~ : bash — Konsole"}
{"ts":"2026-11-15T17:20:02.348Z","app":"org.kde.konsole","type":"key","key":"H","mods":["shift"],"window":"~ : bash — Konsole"}
```

# CLAUDE.md — instructions for coding agents working on `brain`

`brain` is a Rust CLI for the Endpoint "Shadow Assistant" home assignment
(`Endpoint Home Assignment.pdf`, not committed). One binary, two commands:
`brain run` captures keystrokes + focus and stores them; `brain query`
(`search`, `text`) answers questions while `run` keeps going.

Design doc (source of truth for architecture):
https://claude.ai/artifact/UTxCHmXHeSBaQASSNNiSP9 — `PLAN.md` is the in-repo
research/architecture write-up and must stay consistent with the code.

## Target platform

Ubuntu, **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Not GNOME. Keys come from evdev
(`/dev/input/event*`, user in the `input` group), resolved with libxkbcommon
(`libxkbcommon.so.0`, linked by file name, so no `-dev` package is needed).
Focus comes from a KWin script calling back over D-Bus. `/dev/uinput` is
root-only on the dev machine: tests must not depend on it. Use
`brain run --synthetic RATE` (hidden flag) to drive the real pipeline without
hardware.

## Hard requirements (from the assignment) — never regress these

- Capture is invisible: no input lag (we never grab devices), **≤ 1 % average
  CPU while typing, ≤ 32 MB RSS**, keeps working after sleep/wake.
- `kill -9` of `run` at any moment + restart ⇒ no corruption
  (`tests/crash_safety.rs` must stay green).
- `query` works while `run` writes and always sees a consistent state.
- Both commands take `--data-dir` (default `./brain-data`) and exit non-zero
  with a message on stderr on error. Query output is JSON on stdout.

## Decisions already made by the owner — do not re-litigate

- `brain query text` returns the **raw decoded keystroke stream** (no
  backspace/cursor editing applied) over a window: default last 10 min,
  `--at T` = 10-min window ending at T, or `--from/--to`.
- Sessions: keyed by (app, window); close after 30 s idle in that context or
  on Enter in single-line contexts; focus loss alone never closes a session.
- Reconstruction tiers: 0 = generic buffer replay, 1 = per-app rules,
  2 = VS Code real-app replay, **opt-in** via `brain run --vscode-replay`,
  falling back to tier 0. Sessions, reconstruction and indexing are built
  before `brain query` (owner's call, changing the original stage order).
- Search is substring matching (FTS5 trigram, case- and accent-insensitive),
  not the design's porter stemming: `run` must find "rerun", `בית` "בבית".
- Sessions and their text must stay a pure function of the log: the crash
  test compares the live index with a fresh rebuild.
- Work proceeds in 4 stages (capture, query, reconstruction, E2E tests).
  After each stage: build, run, test it yourself, report, then **stop and
  wait for explicit approval** before the next stage.

## Code map

```
src/main.rs              CLI (clap), error → stderr + exit 1
src/capture/mod.rs       `run` orchestration: sources, ingest thread, signals
src/capture/input.rs     poll loop over evdev devices, hotplug, EVIOCSMASK
src/capture/keys.rs      pure key processing: xkb resolution + repeat synthesis
src/capture/xkb.rs       libxkbcommon FFI wrapper
src/capture/recorder.rs  stamps focus, appends to log, clipboard on paste, lock pause
src/capture/desktop.rs   D-Bus: KWin focus script, Klipper, lock, sleep, layouts
src/capture/synthetic.rs synthetic input source for tests/benchmarks
src/eventlog.rs          append-only JSONL log: torn-tail repair, line reader
src/store.rs             SQLite schema (WAL, FTS5), helpers
src/ingest.rs            log → SQLite, offset advanced in the same transaction
src/sessions.rs          session rules, open/close, live text, crash recovery
src/query.rs             `query search` / `query text`, time windows, JSON output
src/reconstruct/         buffer.rs tier 0 · apps.rs + editor.rs tier 1 ·
                         tier2.rs + vscode/ tier 2 (VS Code replay, opt-in)
src/event.rs, timefmt.rs event format, timestamp parsing/formatting
tests/                   integration tests that drive the real binary
```

## Working rules

- **No backward compatibility.** This is the first robust version, still
  being built: change the log format, the schema or the CLI freely, with no
  migration, compatibility shims or legacy-format handling. Test data
  directories can be deleted and recreated.

- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` (zero warnings) and `cargo test`
  before every commit. Run `cargo test --release --test crash_safety` when
  touching the log, ingest or store.
- Keep the hot path (input thread) free of allocation-heavy work, blocking
  I/O other than the single log `write(2)`, and SQLite.
- The log is the ground truth; SQLite is derived and rebuildable. Never put
  data only in SQLite.
- Commit messages per https://cbea.ms/git-commit/ (imperative subject
  ≤ 50 chars, blank line, body wrapped at 72 explaining what and why).
  Commit at meaningful checkpoints.
- Prefer verifying behaviour by running the binary over reasoning about it;
  report exactly what was tested and what was not.
- Tests that need VS Code are `#[ignore]`: `cargo test --release --test
  vscode_replay --test tier2_e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1`.
- `tests/repeat_e2e.rs` (`#[ignore]`) types into a real Kate window through
  /dev/uinput: it needs the KDE session, `scripts/setup-test-permissions.sh`,
  and nobody touching the keyboard or mouse while it runs.
- The input loop must deliver key transitions before emitting the repeats
  due at the same time (`keys::tests::ticking_past_an_unread_release_adds_repeats`).
- Never change desktop session state you did not set up (lock/unlock,
  suspend); check it first and restore it.

content.content:
## Sessions and reconstruction

Ingest (inside `brain run`, about once a second) turns the log into
**writing sessions**, stored in the `sessions` table with an FTS5 index.

* A session is one `(app, window title)`. Markers that change while you
  type are removed from the title first: an editor's unsaved-file dot or
  `*`, and the spinner glyphs terminal programs animate (`◐ ◑ ⠹ ✳`).
  When the title changes *because of the typing* (VS Code names a new file
  after its first line, a mail window after its subject), the session
  continues: a change of the *same* window's title (KWin tells a title
  change from a window activation) within 1 s of a keystroke in it, with no
  shortcut in between, is treated as a rename. It closes after **30 s without
  typing in that window**, or right away when a single-line field is
  submitted (Enter at a shell prompt, in a chat box or a browser's address
  bar), cancelled (Ctrl+C at a prompt), or left for another field of the
  same window (Tab, Ctrl+L in a browser). Switching to another app and back
  within 30 s continues the same session. Stopping or restarting `brain run`
  closes all sessions.
* While a session is open, its text so far is already in the index, so a
  search finds what you are typing right now.
* **Tier 0**: keys are replayed into a virtual text field with a cursor,
  selection, word-wise movement and deletion, and undo/redo. Only keyboard
  cursor movement is followed (see "Decisions and edge cases").
* **Tier 1**: a small table of app classes decides what keys mean. In
  terminals: readline shortcuts (Ctrl+A/E/U/K/W) and Up/Down history recall
  from the commands `brain` saw you run. In browsers: Tab and Ctrl+L/K/T/W
  move to another field. Enter submits single-line fields and inserts a
  newline elsewhere. Editors and unknown apps keep their document across
  sessions. Single-line fields start empty each time.
* **Tier 2** (`--vscode-replay`): when a VS Code session closes, its
  keystrokes are replayed into a headless VS Code with your settings, in a
  network-less sandbox with capped CPU and memory. The session text then
  comes from VS Code itself (auto-indent, bracket pairs, your keybindings).
  The session stores the changed lines. If replay is impossible or fails,
  the tier 0/1 text stays.

Inspect the result:

```sh
sqlite3 ~/brain-data/brain.db \
  "SELECT id, app, started_at, ended_at, status, end_reason, tier_used, reconstructed_text FROM sessions"
```

## Decisions and edge cases
## Where the agent failed

This project was built by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) with the owner reviewing
every stage. These are the mistakes it made, in order, and how they were
caught. Transcripts are in `ai-logs/`.

1. **Wrong library assumption.** It wrote D-Bus code for zbus 6 with a
   feature that does not exist there; the build failed and it moved to
   zbus 5.
2. **A commit that did not build.** The first commit declared a module
   that was only added in the next one. Caught by building each commit
   in a clean worktree; the history was rewritten before anything was
   pushed.
3. **A background agent's PLAN.md described things that were never
   built** (a "durable offset", timerfds, text session ids, an in-memory
   index for open sessions). It was kept out of the repo until it can be
   rewritten against the code.
4. **Unlocking the owner's screen.** To test lock handling it ran
   `loginctl lock-session` and `unlock-session` without first checking the
   screen state. The screen was already locked (the owner was away), so it
   unlocked the machine for 23 seconds before noticing and re-locking it.
   It now checks and restores desktop state before such tests.
5. **A sleep/wake test that could not work.** `rtcwake -m mem` suspends
   behind logind's back, so brain (correctly) saw nothing. The test was
   redone through `systemctl suspend`.
6. **Bugs only found on the owner's real data**, not by its own tests:
   shortcuts on the Hebrew layout logged as Hebrew letters (so Ctrl+V was
   not recognised as paste), text leaking between Chrome tabs that share
   the title "New tab", an animated terminal title (Claude Code's own
   spinner) splitting a session every second, VS Code's new-file title

content.content:
1:## Decisions and edge cases
2:
3:**Platform and capture**
4:* **Linux, KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland.** Wayland gives applications no way
5:  to observe other apps' keystrokes, so `brain` reads the kernel's input
6:  devices (evdev) passively: read-only, never grabbed, so it cannot add
7:  input lag. Focus (app + window title) comes from a small KWin script
8:  that calls `brain` over D-Bus. PLAN.md compares the alternatives.
9:* **Keys are resolved at capture time** with libxkbcommon and your real
10:  layouts (us/il, Alt+Shift switching, layout changes from the tray), so
11:  the log holds the characters the app received (`"ש"`, `"H"`), as in the
12:  assignment's example event. Key repeat is regenerated on KDE's schedule.
13:* **Held keys** are logged with the repeats KDE's schedule produces
14:  (600 ms delay, then 25 Hz), exactly. The app may still have received one
15:  more or one fewer character per hold: on Wayland each app runs its own
16:  repeat timer, and Qt apps use timers that may fire up to 5% early or late
17:  (a 600 ms delay fires anywhere in ~570–630 ms). Measured against Kate, the
18:  same 620 ms hold gave 1, 2 or 3 characters across runs; brain's
19:  reconstruction stays within one character per hold (two for holds over
20:  2 s). `tests/repeat_e2e.rs` measures this against a real Kate window.
21:* **Shortcuts are logged on the Latin layout** (Ctrl+A, not Ctrl+ש), the
22:  way applications match them; this also makes paste detection work in
23:  Hebrew.
24:* **Paste** (Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Shift+V, Shift+Insert): the clipboard text is
25:  read from Klipper at that moment and logged, up to 64 KiB.
26:* **Screen lock pauses capture**, so the unlock password is never logged.
27:* **Sleep/wake**: on resume (logind's PrepareForSleep signal) all
28:  keyboards are reopened. Tested with a real suspend.
29:* **The mouse is not captured.** `brain` reads keyboards only. A mouse
30:  click can move the text cursor, but its position on screen tells `brain`
31:  nothing about where in the text the cursor went, so reconstruction cannot
32:  use it. Tiers 0/1 (and tier 2) therefore **do not support text edited
33:  after the cursor was moved with the mouse** (clicking into the middle of a
34:  line to fix a typo, selecting with the mouse, drag and drop): typing
35:  continues from where the *keyboard* last left the cursor. Cursor moves
36:  with the keyboard (arrows, Home/End, Ctrl+arrows, Shift+selection,
37:  Ctrl+A) are followed.
38:
39:**Storage**
40:* **The JSONL log is the ground truth; SQLite is derived.** Capture only
41:  appends one line per event (never blocks on SQLite). Ingest builds the
42:  index from the log once a second, in one transaction together with the
43:  log offset, so a crash never duplicates or skips anything. Deleting
44:  `brain.db` rebuilds it from the log. Raw keystrokes are not copied into
45:  SQLite.
46:* **`query text` assumes the log is in time order.** It starts reading at
47:  the last checkpoint before its window and stops 60 s of log after it. If
48:  the system clock is stepped backwards while capturing (an NTP correction,
49:  a manual change), keys typed after the step whose times fall in a queried
50:  window can be missed. PLAN.md (section 10) describes an exact bound.
51:* **No backward compatibility yet.** This is the first version: a database
52:  with another schema version is refused (delete it to rebuild).
53:
54:**Sessions and reconstruction**
55:* **Session key `(app, window title)`**, with markers that change while
56:  typing removed from the title (unsaved-file dots, terminal spinners), and
57:  titles renamed by the typing itself followed as the same session. Another
58:  window being activated is never a rename; but switching *tabs* of the
59:  same window with the mouse (invisible to brain) within 1 s of the last
60:  keystroke would wrongly count as one.
61:* **30 s idle per window; focus loss alone never ends a session.** Enter
62:  ends a session only in single-line fields (shell prompts, chat boxes,
63:  browser address/search bars, launchers such as KRunner, by app class);
64:  elsewhere it is a newline.
65:  In browsers, Shift+Enter is a newline.
66:* **Single-line fields start each session empty**; editors keep their
67:  document across sessions. Window titles of single-line fields are
68:  reused by unrelated fields ("New tab", "~"), so carrying text over would
69:  mix them.
70:* **Reconstruction is incremental**: each key is applied once to the open
71:  session's in-memory buffer, and open sessions' text is refreshed in the
72:  index every second, so search sees what is being typed now. (The design
73:  reconstructed at close and rebuilt open sessions at query time; the
74:  result is the same, the cost is not.) VS Code tier 2 runs at close.
75:* **Unknown cursor = end of the text**: after `brain run` restarts, and at
76:  the start of a VS Code replay.
77:* **Shell history recall** (Up) uses only the commands `brain` saw being
78:  run in that terminal app; history from before, tab completion and shell
79:  autosuggestions (zsh) are not visible, so those lines can be wrong.
80:* **Sessions that changed nothing leave no row** (cursor movement only, a
81:  typo typed and deleted, whitespace).
82:* **`query text` is the raw stream, `search` the edited text.** As the
83:  owner decided, `text` returns exactly what was typed (with `<Backspace>`
84:  and other keys visible) rather than reconstructed text; reconstructed,
85:  edit-aware text is what `search` matches and returns.
86:* **Search matches substrings.** The index uses SQLite FTS5's trigram
87:  tokenizer: a query word matches anywhere inside a word, ignoring case and
88:  accents (`run` finds "running" and "rerun", `בית` finds "בבית", `cafe`
89:  finds "Café"). This replaces the design's English-only porter stemmer,
90:  which cannot find Hebrew words with attached prefixes. Query words
91:  shorter than 3 characters cannot use the trigram index.
92:* **VS Code tier 2 is opt-in** (`--vscode-replay`): it needs the file's
93:  content at session start (snapshot within 10 s, no unsaved changes),
94:  costs ~25 s for the first replay and ~1.2 GB while VS Code runs (capped,
95:  outside brain's budget), and runs with extensions disabled when your
96:  extensions exceed 300 MB. Suggestion acceptance may not replay the same.
97:
98:**Running**
99:* **Service as you, not root**: a systemd user service, because desktop
100:  integration needs your session's D-Bus, and a root keylogger is the
101:  worst case if it is ever compromised.
102:
103:## Tests

content.text:
`brain query text` reads the raw keystrokes straight from the log, not from the sessions table, and prints one app's stream for a time window. Here are the steps, following `query::text` in `src/query.rs`:

**1. Parse the CLI** (`src/main.rs`)
- `--app A` is required. `--at`, `--from` and `--to` are optional. `--at` can't be combined with the other two, which clap enforces.
- It checks that the data folder and `brain.db` exist, and stops with an error if not.
- It takes "now" once, so every relative time in the command uses the same reference.

**2. Work out the window** (`resolve`)
- Each time flag is parsed: relative (`-2h`), local (`14:00`, `2026-11-17 09:00`), or RFC 3339.
- Then:

| Flags | Window |
|---|---|
| none | the last 10 minutes |
| `--at T` | T − 10 min … T |
| `--from A` | A … now |
| `--to B` | B − 10 min … B |
| `--from A --to B` | A … B |

- If the window starts after it ends, that's an error.

**3. Read two things from the database**, read-only:
- **Where to start in the log:** the byte position of the latest bookmark at or before the window's start (`log_checkpoints`). Bookmarks are at most 5 s apart, so reading starts at most 5 s before the window.
- **The known apps:** every distinct app id in `sessions`. These are candidates for resolving `--app`.

**4. Read the log forward** from that byte (`LogReader`, which returns only complete lines, never one still being written):
- Lines that don't parse are skipped.
- **It stops** at the first event more than 60 s past the window's end. That margin allows for small clock wobbles.
- **It keeps** only events that are inside the window, are typing (a key or a paste), and whose app id contains the `--app` text, ignoring case.
- Each kept event is held in memory together with its app id, and each such app is added to the candidate list.
- Focus, lock and sleep events are ignored.

**5. Resolve `--app` to one app** (`resolve_app`), among the apps with sessions plus those that typed in the window:
- An exact match wins, ignoring case: `code` is `code`, even though `com.microsoft.VSCode` also contains it.
- Otherwise, the one id that contains the text.
- **Several matches are an error** listing them, so two apps' streams are never mixed. **No match is an error** too: it lists the known apps, or says nothing has been typed yet.

**6. Render that app's events in log order** (`render_key`), with no editing applied:

| Event | Output |
|---|---|
| a typed character (Shift/AltGr already applied: `H`, `ש`, `€`) | the character |
| Enter / Tab | a newline / a tab |
| any other key | `<Backspace>`, `<Left>`, `<Delete>`, … |
| a shortcut | `<Ctrl+V>`, `<Ctrl+Shift+V>`, `<Alt+Tab>` |
| a paste | the pasted text, inline |

Held-key repeats are included, because the app received them. So a held Backspace shows as several `<Backspace>`.

**7. Print the JSON**, with times in local time:
```json
{
  "app": "org.kde.konsole",
  "at": null,
  "from": "2026-11-17T10:00:00.000+02:00",
  "to": "2026-11-17T10:10:00.000+02:00",
  "text": "git staus<Backspace><Backspace>tus\n"
}
```
`app` is the full id, and `from`/`to`/`at` echo the window that was actually used.

**While `brain run` is writing:** the bookmark comes from a consistent database snapshot. The log reader never returns a half-written line. Lines appended after the read started may or may not be included, which is fine either way. Events from the last second, not yet ingested, are still read because they're in the log.

**Cost:** about the window's length plus at most 5 s of log is read, so a 10-minute query reads about 10 minutes of log whatever its total size. Only that app's matching events are held in memory.

**Limitations:**
- If the system clock is stepped backwards while capturing, keys typed after that point can be missed. That's the "time order" assumption we discussed; it's documented.
- An app that never had a session and typed nothing in the window can't be resolved. Asking for it is an error, though nothing would be printed for it anyway.

content.text:
To confirm what I'm changing: until now `query text` returned the raw stream, as you'd originally decided. From now on it returns **reconstructed** text, built with the same session and reconstruction code `search` uses. No second implementation.

**What `text` will return:** the app's text **as it stood at the end of the window**.
- **Sessions that ended inside the window:** their stored final text, as already in the database (tier 2 included).
- **Sessions still running at the end of the window**, e.g. `--at 10:05` when you kept typing until 10:20: the session is replayed from its start up to 10:05 through the same engine. You get exactly what was written at 10:05, not later edits.
- **Editors (multi-line):** each later session continues the previous one's document, so only the latest state of each document is shown, not every intermediate copy.
- **Single-line fields:** each session is its own entry (a command, a search, a chat message), so all of them in the window are listed, in order.
- **Output:** a `text` field joining everything, plus a `sessions` list with each part's id, window title and times.

**How it avoids duplicating code:** to replay a session to a point in time, the engine needs the document the session started from. Today that's only available for sessions still open, which crash recovery uses via `context_state`. I'll store each session's starting state (text, cursor, selection) in its row. Then crash recovery and "text at T" become **the same replay function**, called with different bounds. Recovery gets simpler too. This changes the schema (v5), so your `brain.db` gets rebuilt from the log.

The raw rendering (`<Backspace>`, `<Ctrl+V>`) goes away entirely.

Here's the recovery code I'll turn into the shared replay:

content.content:
* **`search`**: sessions whose text contains *every* word, anywhere inside
  a word, in any case (`run` finds "rerun", `בית` finds "בבית"), newest
  first (default limit 20). Open sessions are included with what has been
  typed so far (`ended_at: null`).
* **`text`**: the raw stream typed into the app, as captured, with no
  editing applied: characters as typed, Enter as a newline, Tab as a tab,
  other keys and shortcuts by name (`<Backspace>`, `<Left>`, `<Ctrl+V>`),
  pasted text inline.
* **`--app A`** can be part of the app id, ignoring case (`--app chrome`
    {
      "session_id": "1",
      "app": "synthetic",
      "window": "corpus.txt",
      "started_at": "2026-11-16T16:51:14.684+02:00",
      "ended_at": null,
      "snippet": "the migration is blocked on the schema change. Dana a…"
    }
  ]
}
```
 (evdev,         │ xkbcommon      ▲ app + window                │ ~1 s
  passive)       │ key repeat     │ from KWin                   ▼
                 ▼                │                       ingest thread ──► brain.db (SQLite WAL)
 KWin script ──D-Bus──────────────┘                         │ sessions        sessions + FTS5 (trigram)
 Klipper (paste text), screen lock, sleep, layouts ─────────┘ reconstruction  context_state
                                                              checkpoints     log_checkpoints
                                    tier 2 worker (opt-in): VS Code replay ──┘
 brain query search ──► brain.db (read-only snapshot)
 brain query text   ──► log_checkpoints → events.jsonl
```

* **Capture** reads keyboards directly from the kernel (evdev), passively, and
  resolves each key to the character the app receives with libxkbcommon and
  the user's real layouts. Focus (app id and window title) comes from a KWin
  script calling back over D-Bus. Every event is one JSON line appended to
  `events.jsonl`.
* **Ingest** (a thread in the same process) tails the log about once a
  second. In one SQLite transaction per batch it writes log checkpoints,
  opens, updates and closes writing sessions, reconstructs their text, and
  advances the log offset. The log is the ground truth; the database is
  derived from it and can be rebuilt from it.

Once a second, the ingest thread syncs the log and runs steps of at most 5,000
lines until it has caught up. **Each step is one SQLite transaction** that
holds everything derived from those lines and the new log offset:

1. read complete lines from `ingest_state.log_offset`;
2. write a log checkpoint at most every 5 s of log time;
3. feed each event to the session engine (section 4);
4. once caught up, close sessions idle on the wall clock, write finished tier
   2 results, refresh the live text of open sessions;
5. store the new offset and commit.
| with sessions open | open sessions are rebuilt from the database and their events replayed from the log (section 4.5); the restart's `start` event then closes them |

`tests/crash_safety.rs` kills brain 25 times under load and checks database
integrity, offsets on line boundaries, a complete log, and that every session,
document and checkpoint equals a clean rebuild from the log.

## 4. Sessions and reconstruction
- **`sessions_fts`**: FTS5 over `reconstructed_text`, external content (the
  text is stored once, in `sessions`), kept in sync by insert/update/delete
  triggers in the same transaction.
- **`context_state`**: each multi-line window's document between sessions.
- **`ingest_state`**: the single log offset.
- **`log_checkpoints`**: `(ts, byte_offset)`, at most one per 5 s of log time.

There are no migrations (first version): a database from another schema
version is refused with a message to delete it.

### 5.3 Why SQLite, WAL and FTS5

- **WAL**: one writer (ingest) never blocks readers, and each `brain query`
  sees a snapshot as of the start of its read: never a half-written session.
- **`synchronous = NORMAL`**: no fsync per commit. A power loss can drop the
  last commits but never corrupts the database, and the dropped work is
  re-derived from the log because the offset rolls back with it.
- **FTS5** is in SQLite itself (bundled, no server), and external content
  avoids storing session text twice.
- A 1 MiB page cache keeps the writer inside the memory budget.

### 5.4 Tokenizer: trigram

The index uses FTS5's **trigram** tokenizer, case- and accent-insensitive: a
query word matches anywhere inside a word (`run` finds "rerun", `cafe` finds
"Café"). *Differs from the design* (porter stemming), on the owner's call:
search should behave as "contains", and porter is English-only, while
trigram finds Hebrew words with attached prefixes (`בית` in "בבית"). Words
shorter than 3 characters cannot use the trigram index and are matched with
`LIKE`.

### 5.5 Log checkpoints

`query text` must read raw keys from the log for a time window without
scanning it from the start. Each checkpoint says "the event at this byte has
this timestamp". Because the log is written in time order, starting at the
latest checkpoint at or before the window misses nothing, and reads at most
5 s of log before the window; reading stops 60 s of log after it. Per-app
checkpoints would not save work, since the log interleaves apps and the
window has to be read anyway. Clock steps backwards are discussed in section
10.

## 6. Query semantics

(`src/query.rs`)

- **`brain query search "<words>" [--app A] [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]
  [--limit N]`**: sessions whose text contains every word (substrings, any
  case), newest first, default limit 20, with a snippet around the first
  match. Open sessions are included with their live text and

* **Capture** reads keyboards directly from the kernel (evdev), passively, and
  resolves each key to the character the app receives with libxkbcommon and
  the user's real layouts. Focus (app id and window title) comes from a KWin
  script calling back over D-Bus. Every event is one JSON line appended to
  `events.jsonl`.
* **Ingest** (a thread in the same process) tails the log about once a
  second. In one SQLite transaction per batch it writes log checkpoints,
  opens, updates and closes writing sessions, reconstructs their text, and
  advances the log offset. The log is the ground truth; the database is
  derived from it and can be rebuilt from it.

Once a second, the ingest thread syncs the log and runs steps of at most 5,000
lines until it has caught up. **Each step is one SQLite transaction** that
holds everything derived from those lines and the new log offset:

1. read complete lines from `ingest_state.log_offset`;
2. write a log checkpoint at most every 5 s of log time;
3. feed each event to the session engine (section 4);
4. once caught up, close sessions idle on the wall clock, write finished tier
   2 results, refresh the live text of open sessions;
5. store the new offset and commit.

document and checkpoint equals a clean rebuild from the log.

## 4. Sessions and reconstruction
- **`sessions_fts`**: FTS5 over `reconstructed_text`, external content (the
  text is stored once, in `sessions`), kept in sync by insert/update/delete
  triggers in the same transaction.
- **`context_state`**: each multi-line window's document between sessions.
- **`ingest_state`**: the single log offset.
- **`log_checkpoints`**: `(ts, byte_offset)`, at most one per 5 s of log time.

There are no migrations (first version): a database from another schema
version is refused with a message to delete it.

### 5.3 Why SQLite, WAL and FTS5

- **WAL**: one writer (ingest) never blocks readers, and each `brain query`
  sees a snapshot as of the start of its read: never a half-written session.
- **`synchronous = NORMAL`**: no fsync per commit. A power loss can drop the
  last commits but never corrupts the database, and the dropped work is
  re-derived from the log because the offset rolls back with it.
- **FTS5** is in SQLite itself (bundled, no server), and external content
  avoids storing session text twice.
- A 1 MiB page cache keeps the writer inside the memory budget.

### 5.4 Tokenizer: trigram

The index uses FTS5's **trigram** tokenizer, case- and accent-insensitive: a
query word matches anywhere inside a word (`run` finds "rerun", `cafe` finds
"Café"). *Differs from the design* (porter stemming), on the owner's call:
search should behave as "contains", and porter is English-only, while
trigram finds Hebrew words with attached prefixes (`בית` in "בבית"). Words
shorter than 3 characters cannot use the trigram index and are matched with
`LIKE`.

### 5.5 Log checkpoints

`query text` must read raw keys from the log for a time window without
scanning it from the start. Each checkpoint says "the event at this byte has
this timestamp". Because the log is written in time order, starting at the
latest checkpoint at or before the window misses nothing, and reads at most
5 s of log before the window; reading stops 60 s of log after it. Per-app
checkpoints would not save work, since the log interleaves apps and the
window has to be read anyway. Clock steps backwards are discussed in section
10.

end of the window instead of the raw keystroke stream: each session of
the app active in the window, at that moment. Sessions that ended in
time contribute their stored text; a session still running is replayed
from the log up to the end of the window. In editors only the latest
state of each document is kept (later sessions continue the earlier
ones); single-line fields are each listed. The output keeps `text`
(the parts, one per line) and adds `sessions` with each part's window
and times.

document it started from (schema v5), so the replay crash recovery
already did becomes one function, `Sessions::replay`, used both by
recovery (open sessions, up to the ingested offset) and by the new
`sessions::text_at` (one session, up to a time). Recovery no longer
depends on context_state for this, which also removes its write-back.

The raw renderer is gone, and so are the log checkpoints: only the raw
`text` read the log by time, so nothing used them any more, and the
documented clock-jump limitation of that read goes with them.

`query text` now returns reconstructed text, built with the same engine as `search` and crash recovery; no reconstruction code is duplicated. Everything is pushed (`eb0da31`, then the `ai-logs/` refresh `fe7c229`).

**What it returns:** the app's text as it stood at the end of the window.
- **A session that ended inside the window** contributes its stored final text.
- **A session still running at the end of the window** is replayed from the log up to that moment, so `--at 11:50:28` shows exactly what was there then, not later edits. In the live check, the editor queried at "4 s ago" showed its text up to that point, with the typo the typist had corrected already gone.
- **Editors:** each later session continues the previous one's document, so only the latest state of each document is shown.
- **Single-line fields** (commands, searches, messages) are each listed in order. Konsole gave `git status`, `cargo test`, `ls -la`, `git status`.
- **Output:** `text` joins the parts one per line. A new `sessions` list gives each part's id, window, start and end. `ended_at` is `null` if the session was still running at the end of the window.

**How duplication was avoided:** each session row now stores the document it started from (text, cursor, selection). Crash recovery's replay became one shared function that works two ways:
- **Crash recovery:** all open sessions, up to what has been ingested.
- **`text`:** one session, up to a point in time.

Recovery got simpler as a side effect: it no longer depends on `context_state`.

**Removed, since nothing uses it any more:**
- The raw renderer (`<Backspace>`, `<Ctrl+V>`).
- The log bookmarks (`log_checkpoints`). Only the raw `text` read the log by time.
- The clock-jump limitation, which only affected that read.

**Tests:**
- **New unit test:** a session part-way through and at its end, a later session continuing a document, and a still-open session.
- **CLI tests rewritten for the new output:**
  - "secret", typed and deleted, doesn't appear.
  - Two Kate sessions give only the final document.
  - `--at` in the middle of a running session gives the partial text.
  - Commands, pastes, local times, full app ids and the error cases.
- **Results:** 119 unit tests, crash safety, `query_cli` and `perf_budget` all pass, and clippy is clean.

**Docs:** README, PLAN.md, CLAUDE.md and the `text` help all describe the new behavior, with the earlier raw output noted as changed at your request.

The schema is now version 5, so rebuild once:
```
! rm ~/brain-data/brain.db && make
```

3. Read the log forward. Keep the typing events (keys and pastes) inside the window whose app matches, and resolve `--app` to one full id.
4. Output `{app, at, from, to, text}`. Same fields, local times.

- `editor::action(class, key, mods)` turns each key into an action.
- `FieldEditor::apply` applies it to a `TextBuffer`.
- `FieldEditor::paste` inserts pasted text.
- `editor::key_suppresses_paste` drops the paste after a plain Ctrl+V in a terminal.

**Putting it together:**
- **One text field per window title** (normalized), so typing in two Kate documents isn't merged.
- **An action that ends the field** (Enter in a terminal or browser, Ctrl+C at a prompt, Tab or Ctrl+L in a browser) closes that field's text as one part, and the next keys start a new empty field. That's the same thing the session engine does.
- **Shell history (Up/Down)** recalls the lines already submitted earlier in the same window of the query, so no database lookup is needed.

Here's a worked example on one log that covers several sessions. All times are local (+02:00).

## What was typed (10:00–10:10)

**Kate, window `notes.md — Kate`, first session (10:00:00–10:00:20)**
```
Shopping list:⏎- milk⏎- breadd⌫
```
After this, nothing is typed in `notes.md` for over 30 s, so the database closes session 1.

**Kate, window `todo.md — Kate` (10:01)**
```
TODO: call Dana⏎⇥send the "Q3" report⏎path: C:\temp
```
(⇥ = Tab, and the quotes and backslash are typed as normal keys.)

**Kate, window `notes.md — Kate`, second session (10:03).** The database records this as a separate session.
```
Ctrl+Home  ↓  End  Ctrl+⌫  oat milk          ← replaces "milk" with "oat milk"
Ctrl+End  ⏎  - 
Alt+Shift  קפה  Alt+Shift                     ← Hebrew, then back to English
Ctrl+V  (clipboard: " ☕ x2")  Ctrl+Z          ← pasted, then undone
 x2
```
The window title briefly becomes `notes.md * — Kate` while unsaved. It normalizes to `notes.md — Kate`, so it's the same window.

**Konsole, window `~` (10:05)**
```
git stauts⌫⌫⌫tus⏎
↑ -s⏎                          ← Up recalls "git status"
rm -rf build Ctrl+C            ← abandoned at the prompt
echo "שלום" > out.txt⏎
```

## Query 1: Kate over the whole range
`brain query text --app kate --from 10:00 --to 10:10`
```json
{
  "app": "org.kde.kate",
  "at": null,
  "from": "2026-11-17T10:00:00.000+02:00",
  "to": "2026-11-17T10:10:00.000+02:00",
  "text": "Shopping list:\n- oat milk\n- bread\n- קפה x2\nTODO: call Dana\n\tsend the \"Q3\" report\npath: C:\\temp",
  "windows": [
    {
      "window": "notes.md — Kate",
      "text": "Shopping list:\n- oat milk\n- bread\n- קפה x2"
    },
    {
      "window": "todo.md — Kate",
      "text": "TODO: call Dana\n\tsend the \"Q3\" report\npath: C:\\temp"
    }
  ]
}
```
- **Sessions don't matter.** `notes.md` was two sessions in the database, but `text` runs all of that window's keys in the range through one text field. So the second session's edits apply to the first session's text: "milk" becomes "oat milk", and the new line is added below.
- **Edits are applied:** `breadd⌫` gives `bread`, Ctrl+⌫ deletes the word, and the undone paste disappears completely, emoji included.
- **Windows are kept apart** and ordered by their first keystroke in the range.
- **Special characters are JSON-escaped as usual:** a newline is `\n`, a Tab `\t`, a quote `\"`, a backslash `\\`. Hebrew and emoji appear as-is (UTF-8).

## Query 2: the same Kate keys, starting after the first session
`brain query text --app kate --from 10:02 --to 10:10`
```json
{
  "app": "org.kde.kate",
  "at": null,
  "from": "2026-11-17T10:02:00.000+02:00",
  "to": "2026-11-17T10:10:00.000+02:00",
  "text": "oat milk\n- קפה x2",
  "windows": [
    { "window": "notes.md — Kate", "text": "oat milk\n- קפה x2" }
  ]
}
```
This shows the "starts empty" limit. The range starts after "Shopping list…" was typed, so `notes.md` starts empty. Ctrl+Home, ↓, End and Ctrl+⌫ have no text to act on, and only what was typed after 10:02 remains. `todo.md` isn't listed because nothing was typed in it after 10:02.

## Query 3: Konsole
`brain query text --app konsole --at 10:10`
```json
{
  "app": "org.kde.konsole",
  "at": "2026-11-17T10:10:00.000+02:00",
  "from": "2026-11-17T10:00:00.000+02:00",
  "to": "2026-11-17T10:10:00.000+02:00",
  "text": "git status\ngit status -s\nrm -rf build\necho \"שלום\" > out.txt",
  "windows": [
    {
      "window": "~",
      "text": "git status\ngit status -s\nrm -rf build\necho \"שלום\" > out.txt"
    }
  ]
}
```
- This uses the terminal adapter. Each Enter submits the line, and the next one starts fresh in the same window's text.
- ↑ recalls `git status` from earlier in this text, and ` -s` is appended to it.
- Ctrl+C abandons a line: it's kept, as written, and the next line starts fresh.
- The database has four separate sessions here, one per Enter or Ctrl+C. `text` doesn't care, since it's one window.
- For comparison, today's raw output for the same range is `git stauts<Backspace><Backspace><Backspace>tus\n<Up> -s\nrm -rf build<Ctrl+C>echo "שלום" > out.txt\n`.

    Text {
## Decisions already made by the owner — do not re-litigate

- `brain query text` returns the **raw decoded keystroke stream** (no
  backspace/cursor editing applied) over a window: default last 10 min,
  `--at T` = 10-min window ending at T, or `--from/--to`. Times accept
  relative (`-2h`), local and RFC 3339 forms. `--app` may be part of the id;
  extensions exceed 300 MB. Suggestion acceptance may not replay the same.

**Queries**
* **`query text` is the raw stream, `search` the edited text.** As the
  owner decided, `text` returns exactly what was typed (with `<Backspace>`
  and other keys visible) rather than reconstructed text; reconstructed,
  edit-aware text is what `search` matches and returns.
* **Search matches substrings.** The index uses SQLite FTS5's trigram
  match. Open sessions are included with their live text and
  `ended_at: null`. A session is in a time window if it overlaps it.
- **`brain query text --app A [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]`**: the raw stream
  typed into the app over the window: characters as typed, Enter as a
  newline, Tab as a tab, other keys and shortcuts by name (`<Backspace>`,
  `<Ctrl+V>`), pasted text inline. No editing is applied (the owner's
  decision: an audit-style trail, distinct from the edited session text).
- **`--app A`** can be part of an app id, ignoring case. `search` keeps

content.text:
`query text` now returns reconstructed text, implemented as we agreed. Only the output step changed; the time window, bookmark seek, log reading and app resolution are as before. Pushed as `4b3b5de`, plus an `ai-logs/` refresh (`1a09bad`).

**The change** (`src/query.rs`):
- `render_key` is gone. A new `reconstruct_windows` splits the selected events by window title (normalized, so `notes.md * — Kate` counts as `notes.md — Kate`).
- It runs each window's events, from an empty text, through the existing tier 0/1 pieces: `classify`, `editor::action`, `FieldEditor::apply` and `paste`, and `key_suppresses_paste`. It only calls them; no reconstruction logic was copied.
- Sessions play no part, so a document edited across several sessions comes out as one text.
- In terminals and other single-line fields, a submit keeps the line and continues on a fresh one, and Up recalls lines submitted earlier in the window.
- The output now has `windows`: each window's text, in order of its first keystroke. `text` joins them one per line.

**Tests:**
- **Three unit tests** run the exact example from my last message through the function, and match it character for character:
  - Kate's two windows, with `notes.md` edited across two sessions: `"Shopping list:\n- oat milk\n- bread\n- קפה x2"` and `"TODO: call Dana\n\tsend the \"Q3\" report\npath: C:\\temp"`. The undone ☕ paste doesn't appear.
  - The same keys from 10:02 on, where `notes.md` starts empty and gives `"oat milk\n- קפה x2"`.
  - Konsole with typo fixing, Up recall and Ctrl+C. It also checks that a plain Ctrl+V doesn't paste in a terminal and an empty Enter adds nothing.
- **A new CLI test** writes the same example to a log and ingests it, confirming the database really holds two `notes.md` sessions. It then runs the three queries through the binary and compares the exact JSON, including how quotes, backslashes, newlines and tabs are escaped and that Hebrew stays readable.
- The existing `text` test expects reconstructed text now (`"the cat sat"`, `"git status"`, `"pasted words"`).
- 123 unit tests, crash safety, the six `query_cli` tests and `perf_budget` all pass, and clippy is clean.

**Docs:**
- The README's query section has the Kate output as its example, with the keystroke table behind it, plus the "from 10:02" and Konsole results.
- PLAN.md, CLAUDE.md and the `text` help describe the reconstruction, and the decisions section notes that the raw output was replaced at your request.

There's no database change this time, so `! make` is enough to use it.

content.content:
## Query

Both commands run while `brain run` is capturing and print JSON. Errors go
to stderr with a non-zero exit code.

```sh
brain query search "migration blocked" [--app A] [--from T] [--to T] [--at T] [--limit N]
brain query text --app A [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]
```

* **`search`**: sessions whose text contains *every* word, anywhere inside
  a word, in any case (`run` finds "rerun", `בית` finds "בבית"), newest
  first (default limit 20). Open sessions are included with what has been
  typed so far (`ended_at: null`).
* **`text`**: what was typed into the app during the window,
  **reconstructed**: the window's keys and pastes, per window title, run
  through the app's tier 0/1 rules (Backspace, selections, undo, Enter
  submitting a shell line, …), each window starting empty at the window's
  start. Sessions play no part: a document edited in several sessions is one
  text. `windows` lists each window's text, ordered by its first keystroke;
  `text` joins them one per line. Edits reaching into text typed before the
  window (Backspace past its start, Ctrl+A) only affect what was typed
  inside it.
* **`--app A`** can be part of the app id, ignoring case (`--app chrome`
  finds `google-chrome`). `search` keeps every app that matches. `text`
  resolves `A` to one app and reports its full id (`"app": "google-chrome"`):
  an exact match wins, otherwise the one id that contains `A`; if several do,
  or none, it is an error that lists them, so text of different apps is
  never mixed.

**Time flags** (both commands): `--at T` is the 10 minutes ending at T;
`--from T` alone runs to now; `--from` and `--to` together are an explicit
window. `--to T` alone means the 10 minutes ending at T for `text`, and
everything up to T for `search`. With no flags, `text` covers the last 10
minutes and `search` all time. T can be:

| Form | Example |
|---|---|
| relative to now | `-30s`, `-15m`, `-2h`, `-1d`, `-1h30m`, `now` |
| local date and time | `"2026-11-16 14:00"`, `2026-11-16T14:00:30` |
| local date (midnight) | `2026-11-16` |
| local time of day (today) | `14:00`, `14:00:30` |
| RFC 3339 with a zone | `2026-11-16T12:00:00Z`, `2026-11-16T14:00:00+02:00` |

Times without a zone are in the local time zone. Output times are local
too, with their offset (`2026-11-17T00:04:38.044+02:00`, still RFC 3339),
and the resolved window is echoed (`from`, `to`, `at`). The log and the
database store UTC.

```json
{
  "query": "migration blocked",
  "from": null,
  "to": null,
  "results": [
    {
      "session_id": "1",
      "app": "synthetic",
      "window": "corpus.txt",
      "started_at": "2026-11-16T16:51:14.684+02:00",
      "ended_at": null,
      "snippet": "the migration is blocked on the schema change. Dana a…"
    }
  ]
}
```

```json
{
  "app": "org.kde.kate",
  "at": null,
  "from": "2026-11-17T10:00:00.000+02:00",
  "to": "2026-11-17T10:10:00.000+02:00",
  "text": "Shopping list:\n- oat milk\n- bread\n- קפה x2\nTODO: call Dana\n\tsend the \"Q3\" report\npath: C:\\temp",
  "windows": [
    {
      "window": "notes.md — Kate",
      "text": "Shopping list:\n- oat milk\n- bread\n- קפה x2"
    },
    {
      "window": "todo.md — Kate",
      "text": "TODO: call Dana\n\tsend the \"Q3\" report\npath: C:\\temp"
    }
  ]
}
```

That is the output for this typing (`tests/query_cli.rs` replays it):

| When | Window | Keys |
|---|---|---|
| 10:00 | `notes.md — Kate` | `Shopping list:⏎- milk⏎- breadd⌫` |
| 10:01 | `todo.md — Kate` | `TODO: call Dana⏎⇥send the "Q3" report⏎path: C:\temp` |
| 10:03 (a new session) | `notes.md * — Kate` | Ctrl+Home `↓` End Ctrl+⌫ `oat milk` Ctrl+End `⏎- קפה` Ctrl+V (`" ☕ x2"`) Ctrl+Z `" x2"` |

With `--from 10:02` instead, `notes.md` starts empty and the result is
`"oat milk\n- קפה x2"`. In Konsole, `git stauts⌫⌫⌫tus⏎`, `↑ -s⏎`,
`rm -rf build` Ctrl+C, `echo "שלום" > out.txt⏎` give
`"git status\ngit status -s\nrm -rf build\necho \"שלום\" > out.txt"`.

brain query text --app A [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]
```

* **`search`**: sessions whose text contains *every* word, anywhere inside
  a word, in any case (`run` finds "rerun", `בית` finds "בבית"), newest
  first (default limit 20). Open sessions are included with what has been
  typed so far (`ended_at: null`).
* **`text`**: what was typed into the app during the window,
  **reconstructed**: the window's keys and pastes, per window title, run
  through the app's tier 0/1 rules (Backspace, selections, undo, Enter
  submitting a shell line, …), each window starting empty at the window's
  start. Sessions play no part: a document edited in several sessions is one
  text. `windows` lists each window's text, ordered by its first keystroke;
  `text` joins them one per line. Edits reaching into text typed before the
  window (Backspace past its start, Ctrl+A) only affect what was typed
  inside it.
* **`--app A`** can be part of the app id, ignoring case (`--app chrome`
  finds `google-chrome`). `search` keeps every app that matches. `text`
  resolves `A` to one app and reports its full id (`"app": "google-chrome"`):
  an exact match wins, otherwise the one id that contains `A`; if several do,
  or none, it is an error that lists them, so text of different apps is
  never mixed.

**Time flags** (both commands): `--at T` is the 10 minutes ending at T;
`--from T` alone runs to now; `--from` and `--to` together are an explicit
window. `--to T` alone means the 10 minutes ending at T for `text`, and
everything up to T for `search`. With no flags, `text` covers the last 10
minutes and `search` all time. T can be:

| Form | Example |
|---|---|
| relative to now | `-30s`, `-15m`, `-2h`, `-1d`, `-1h30m`, `now` |
| local date and time | `"2026-11-16 14:00"`, `2026-11-16T14:00:30` |
| local date (midnight) | `2026-11-16` |
| local time of day (today) | `14:00`, `14:00:30` |
| RFC 3339 with a zone | `2026-11-16T12:00:00Z`, `2026-11-16T14:00:00+02:00` |

Times without a zone are in the local time zone. Output times are local
too, with their offset (`2026-11-17T00:04:38.044+02:00`, still RFC 3339),
and the resolved window is echoed (`from`, `to`, `at`). The log and the
database store UTC.

```json
{
  "query": "migration blocked",
  "from": null,
  "to": null,
  "results": [
    {
      "session_id": "1",
      "app": "synthetic",
      "window": "corpus.txt",
      "started_at": "2026-11-16T16:51:14.684+02:00",
      "ended_at": null,
      "snippet": "the migration is blocked on the schema change. Dana a…"
    }
  ]
}
```

```json
{
  "app": "org.kde.kate",
  "at": null,
  "from": "2026-11-17T10:00:00.000+02:00",
  "to": "2026-11-17T10:10:00.000+02:00",
  "text": "Shopping list:\n- oat milk\n- bread\n- קפה x2\nTODO: call Dana\n\tsend the \"Q3\" report\npath: C:\\temp",
  "windows": [
    {
      "window": "notes.md — Kate",
      "text": "Shopping list:\n- oat milk\n- bread\n- קפה x2"
    },
    {
      "window": "todo.md — Kate",
      "text": "TODO: call Dana\n\tsend the \"Q3\" report\npath: C:\\temp"
    }
  ]
}
```

That is the output for this typing (`tests/query_cli.rs` replays it):

| When | Window | Keys |
|---|---|---|
| 10:00 | `notes.md — Kate` | `Shopping list:⏎- milk⏎- breadd⌫` |
| 10:01 | `todo.md — Kate` | `TODO: call Dana⏎⇥send the "Q3" report⏎path: C:\temp` |
| 10:03 (a new session) | `notes.md * — Kate` | Ctrl+Home `↓` End Ctrl+⌫ `oat milk` Ctrl+End `⏎- קפה` Ctrl+V (`" ☕ x2"`) Ctrl+Z `" x2"` |

With `--from 10:02` instead, `notes.md` starts empty and the result is
`"oat milk\n- קפה x2"`. In Konsole, `git stauts⌫⌫⌫tus⏎`, `↑ -s⏎`,
`rm -rf build` Ctrl+C, `echo "שלום" > out.txt⏎` give
`"git status\ngit status -s\nrm -rf build\necho \"שלום\" > out.txt"`.

content.content:
### 5.5 Log checkpoints

`query text` must read the keys of a time window from the log without
scanning it from the start. Each checkpoint says "the event at this byte has
this timestamp". Because the log is written in time order, starting at the
latest checkpoint at or before the window misses nothing, and reads at most
5 s of log before the window; reading stops 60 s of log after it. Per-app
checkpoints would not save work, since the log interleaves apps and the
window has to be read anyway. Clock steps backwards are discussed in section
10.

## 6. Query semantics
## 9. Testing strategy

- **Unit tests** (about 120, `cargo test`): key resolution and layouts,
  repeat synthesis (including a 300-scenario stress test against an
  independent model, with random early and late wakeups), the recorder, the
  log's torn-tail repair, schema and search, ingest, the tier 0 buffer and
  tier 1 rules, title normalization and renames, every session rule, crash
  recovery after every line, time parsing and query windows.
- **Integration tests run by default**: `crash_safety` (25 `kill -9`s under
  load, compared with a clean rebuild), `query_cli` (the binary's JSON
  output, search semantics through the CLI, time windows, raw text, errors,
  and thousands of queries while `run` writes), `perf_budget` (CPU and
  memory budget).
- **Opt-in tests against real software**: `repeat_e2e` and
  `real_keyboard_e2e` type through a uinput keyboard into real Kate windows
  and compare Kate's saved files with brain (held-key repeats, Hebrew via
  Alt+Shift, focus moving between windows, keyboard unplug/replug);
  `vscode_replay` and `tier2_e2e` drive real VS Code.
- **Manual, once**: sleep/wake through a real suspend, screen lock and
  unlock, the systemd service (start, restart after `kill -9`, clean stop).

## 10. Limitations and future work

content.content:
## Decisions already made by the owner — do not re-litigate

- `brain query text` reconstructs "stupidly": the keys typed in the time
  window, per app and window title, run through the tier 0/1 adapters from
  an empty text (no sessions involved); output `windows` + joined `text`.
  It replaced the earlier raw-keystroke output at the owner's request.
  Window: default last 10 min,
  `--at T` = 10-min window ending at T, or `--from/--to`. Times accept
  relative (`-2h`), local and RFC 3339 forms. `--app` may be part of the id;
  `text` resolves it to exactly one app and reports the full id.
- Sessions: keyed by (app, normalized window title); close after 30 s idle
  in that context or on Enter in single-line contexts; focus loss alone
  never closes a session; a title change of the typed window (a `renamed`
  focus event) shortly after a keystroke keeps the session.
- The mouse is not captured (owner's call): cursor moves made with the mouse
  are a documented limitation, not something to work around.
- Reconstruction tiers: 0 = generic buffer replay, 1 = per-app rules,
  2 = VS Code real-app replay, **opt-in** via `brain run --vscode-replay`,
  falling back to tier 0. Sessions, reconstruction and indexing are built
  before `brain query` (owner's call, changing the original stage order).
- Search is substring matching (FTS5 trigram, case- and accent-insensitive),
  not the design's porter stemming: `run` must find "rerun", `בית` "בבית".
- Sessions and their text must stay a pure function of the log: the crash
  test compares the live index with a fresh rebuild.
- Work went through stages (capture with sessions and indexing, query,
  end-to-end verification), each approved by the owner. Keep the habit for
  new work: build, run, test it yourself, report, then **stop and wait for
  explicit approval** before starting the next piece.

## Code map
**Queries**
* **`query text` reconstructs "stupidly", by window.** It takes the keys
  typed in the time window and runs them through the same tier 0/1 adapters
  the sessions use, per app and window title, from an empty text: no session
  boundaries, no text from before the window. (An earlier version returned
  the raw keys with `<Backspace>` etc.; the owner asked for reconstruction.)
* **Search matches substrings.** The index uses SQLite FTS5's trigram
  tokenizer: a query word matches anywhere inside a word, ignoring case and
  accents (`run` finds "running" and "rerun", `בית` finds "בבית", `cafe`
  finds "Café"). This replaces the design's English-only porter stemmer,
  which cannot find Hebrew words with attached prefixes. Query words
  shorter than 3 characters cannot use the trigram index and are matched
  with a slower scan.
* **Times in, times out are local.** `--from`, `--to` and `--at` accept
  relative times (`-2h`), local dates and times, and RFC 3339; output times
  are local with their offset. The log and the database store UTC.
* **`--app` takes part of the id.** `search` keeps every matching app;
  `text` must resolve to exactly one app and reports its full id, so two
  apps' keystrokes are never mixed into one stream.
* **`query text` assumes the log is in time order.** It starts reading at
  the last checkpoint before its window and stops 60 s of log after it. If
  the system clock is stepped backwards while capturing (an NTP correction,
  a manual change), keys typed after the step whose times fall in a queried
  window can be missed. PLAN.md (section 10) describes an exact bound.

**Running**

- **PLAN.md:** the testing section said the CLI tests cover "raw text". It now says reconstructed text, including the README's example.
- **Module docs:** the reconstruction module now says tiers 0/1 are also used by `query text`.
- **CLAUDE.md:** the `query text` decision is rewrapped and uses the same terms.

**Smoke run on your desktop:** capture started with the keyboard and KWin, a second `run` was refused, queries returned JSON, and the error cases (nothing typed yet, an empty time range, a missing folder) all exited 1 with clear messages. Stopping was clean and returned exit 0.

Run everything from the repo root (`~/Documents/shadow-assistant`). The first build takes about a minute; after that, each suite's time is listed.

## Automated: run by default

```sh
# Everything in one go: unit tests + crash_safety + query_cli + perf_budget (~1 min)
cargo test --release

# Or one suite at a time:
cargo test --release --lib                                # 123 unit tests (<1 s)
cargo test --release --test crash_safety -- --nocapture   # 25 random kill -9s (~20 s)
cargo test --release --test query_cli -- --nocapture      # query commands through the binary (~8 s)
cargo test --release --test perf_budget -- --nocapture    # CPU/memory budget, prints the numbers (~32 s)

# Lint, as required before each commit:
cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy --all-targets
```

## Automated: opt-in, against real software

**Before the Kate tests:** they need the permission script (run once; you already did) and an **unlocked screen**. Keep your **hands off the keyboard and mouse** while they run, because they type into real Kate windows.
```sh
sudo sh scripts/setup-test-permissions.sh          # once; undo with --undo

# Held-key repeats vs. a real Kate window (~22 s), prints a per-hold table:
cargo test --release --test repeat_e2e -- --ignored --nocapture

# Hebrew via Alt+Shift, focus between two Kate windows, keyboard unplug/replug (~13 s):
cargo test --release --test real_keyboard_e2e -- --ignored --nocapture
```

**VS Code tests:** these need VS Code installed. They run headless, so nothing appears on screen and you can keep working.
```sh
cargo test --release --test vscode_replay -- --ignored --test-threads=1   # 12 tests (~4 min)
cargo test --release --test tier2_e2e -- --ignored --nocapture            # end to end through ingest (~25 s)
```

## Manual tests

For each of these, start a test instance in **terminal 1** and leave it running:
```sh
cargo build --release
./target/release/brain run --data-dir /tmp/brain-manual
```
Use **terminal 2** for the steps. In every case, Ctrl+C in terminal 1 should stop it with exit code 0.

**1. Real typing and both queries**
1. Type in a few apps: Konsole (commands with Enter, Backspace, Up), Kate (several lines, Ctrl+Z), Chrome (a search), and some Hebrew via Alt+Shift.

```sh
tail -f /tmp/brain-manual/events.jsonl                       # every key, with app and window

```
Expected: `search` finds the session, and `text` shows the edited text per window, with local times and the full app id.

**2. Paste (Klipper)**
1. Copy some text, then press Ctrl+V in Kate.
2. Check: `grep '"paste"' /tmp/brain-manual/events.jsonl | tail -1`. It should show the clipboard text.
3. In Konsole, plain Ctrl+V shouldn't add text to the session; Ctrl+Shift+V should.

**3. Screen lock**
1. Type a few keys, lock with Meta+L, unlock by typing your password, then type a few more keys.
2. Check: `grep -E '"lock"|"unlock"' /tmp/brain-manual/events.jsonl`. There should be a `lock` and an `unlock` event with **no key events between them**, so your password isn't recorded.

**4. Sleep/wake**
1. Suspend:
```sh
sudo rtcwake -m no -s 30 && systemctl suspend      # wakes by itself after ~30 s
```
2. Unlock and type a few keys.
3. Check: terminal 1 shows `brain: resumed: reopened 1 keyboard(s)`, and `grep '"system"' /tmp/brain-manual/events.jsonl` shows `sleep`, `lock`, `wake`, `unlock`. The keys typed after unlocking should be in the log.

**5. Keyboard layout from the tray**
Switch layout with the tray's keyboard icon (not Alt+Shift). Terminal 1 should print `brain: keyboard layout switched to #1`, and typing should log Hebrew characters.

**6. Keyboard hotplug** (if you have a USB keyboard)
Plug it in, type on it, unplug it, and type on the laptop keyboard. Keys from both should appear in the log, and none should be stuck as Shift.

**7. `kill -9` and restart**
1. Run `pkill -9 -f 'brain run --data-dir /tmp/brain-manual'`.
2. Start terminal 1's command again and type.
3. Check:
   - capture continues;
   - `grep -c '"start"' /tmp/brain-manual/events.jsonl` went up by one;
   - `query search` still finds the text typed before the kill.

1. Stop `brain`, then run `rm /tmp/brain-manual/brain.db`.
2. Start it again.
3. Running the same `query search` and `query text` again should give the same results, rebuilt from the log.

1. Restart terminal 1 with replay on: `./target/release/brain run --vscode-replay --data-dir /tmp/brain-manual`
2. Open a **saved** file in VS Code and type a function with braces and Enter. Stop typing for 30 s or more, so the session closes. The first replay takes about 25 s to start VS Code.

```sh

```

```sh

content.text:
Here's what I'd change. Nothing is touched yet.

**1. Where the service keeps its data**

There's a constraint first: the service runs as you, without root, so it can only write where your user can. A folder outside your home, such as `/var/lib/brain`, would have to be created by root once and handed to your user. A drop-in folder like `~/.config/systemd/user/brain.service.d/` is meant for configuration overrides, not data, so I wouldn't put the capture log there. Two options:

- **A. A state folder that systemd manages** (recommended): `~/.local/state/brain`.
  - The unit declares `StateDirectory=brain` with `StateDirectoryMode=0700`. systemd creates the folder, private to you, before starting `brain`, and passes its path in, so the unit uses `--data-dir %S/brain`.
  - It's the standard place for service data (the XDG state directory), out of sight. Nothing gets added to the top of your home folder.
  - systemd can also remove it itself: `systemctl --user clean brain --what=state`.
- **B. Really outside your home:** `/var/lib/brain-<user>`.
  - `make install-service` would create it once with `sudo` (owned by you, mode 0700), and the unit would point there.
  - It means one more root step, and the folder survives a deleted home directory, which might not be what you want for a keylogger's data.

**2. `make uninstall-service` deletes the data folder**

It would stop and disable the service, then remove the unit file and **the service's data folder** (A: `systemctl --user clean brain --what=state`; B: `sudo rm -rf /var/lib/brain-<user>`). It prints the folder path first, so it's clear what was deleted. `make uninstall`, which removes the binary, stays separate. For keeping the data while removing the service, `make uninstall-service KEEP_DATA=1` would skip the delete.

**3. Docs and tests**
- The README's service section gets the new location and the fact that uninstalling deletes the captured data. The test instructions get updated steps for the service check.
- PLAN.md, the security section, gets the data location.
- I'd test it with a temporary copy of the unit, as before: start, `kill -9` and restart, check the folder is created 0700, then uninstall and check the folder is gone. Your real service install isn't touched.

Which location do you want, A or B? And should `KEEP_DATA=1` exist, or should uninstalling always delete?

content.content:
### As a service

`brain` can run as a **systemd user service**: it starts with your Plasma
session, restarts if it crashes, stops at logout, and runs as you (no
root; it needs your desktop session for focus tracking):

```sh
make install-service          # installs /usr/bin/brain + the unit, enables it
journalctl --user -u brain -f # its messages
systemctl --user stop brain   # pause capture
make uninstall-service        # remove it
```

The service uses `~/brain-data`. Stop it before running `brain run` by hand
on the same directory (only one `brain run` per data directory). The
service runs without `--vscode-replay`; add it to `ExecStart` in
`~/.config/systemd/user/brain.service` to turn it on.

content.text:
Done and pushed (`bd18e51`). The service now keeps its data in its own systemd state folder, and `make uninstall-service` deletes it unless you pass `KEEP_DATA=1`.

**What changed:**
- **`packaging/brain.service`:** `StateDirectory=brain` with mode `0700`. Before each start, systemd creates `~/.local/state/brain`, private to you, and the unit passes it as `--data-dir %S/brain`. Your local edit to that line (`/tmp/service-brain-data`) is replaced by this.
- **`make uninstall-service`:** stops and disables the service, prints the data folder it's deleting, and deletes it with `systemctl --user clean --what=state brain`. Then it removes the unit file.
- **`make uninstall-service KEEP_DATA=1`:** the same, but keeps the data and says so.
- **`make install-service`:** now prints where the data goes.
- **README and PLAN.md:** describe the location, how to point `brain query` at it, and that uninstalling deletes the data.

**Tested** with a temporary copy of the unit (now removed):
- The folder was created as `drwx------`.
- Capture wrote its log and database into it.
- After `kill -9`, systemd restarted the service.
- The clean step deleted the folder.

I also checked both uninstall variants with `make -n`. I didn't run the real `make install-service`, because it needs your sudo password.

Folders from your earlier service runs (`~/brain-data`, `/tmp/service-brain-data`) aren't moved or deleted. Remove them yourself if you don't need them.

**To check it yourself:**
```sh
make install-service
systemctl --user status brain                       # active (running)
ls -ld ~/.local/state/brain                         # drwx------
brain query search "<a word you typed>" --data-dir ~/.local/state/brain
make uninstall-service KEEP_DATA=1                  # service gone, data kept
ls ~/.local/state/brain                             # still there
make install-service && make uninstall-service      # service and data gone
ls ~/.local/state/brain                             # No such file or directory
```

content.text:
I found the cause. Nothing is changed yet.

**Why it was skipped**

In your test database, both VS Code sessions say `skipped: could not identify the file from the window title`:

| Session | Window title | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 40 | `test.txt - ai-logs - Visual Studio Code` | `test.txt` is **outside** the window's folder |
| 39 | `Untitled-1 - ai-logs - Visual Studio Code` | a new, never-saved file: nothing on disk to replay from (correct, but the message is misleading) |

The other sessions, from your normal runs and the service, show no tier-2 status at all. That's expected: those ran without `--vscode-replay`.

**How the file lookup works today:** VS Code's default title gives only the file name and the folder name (`test.txt` and `ai-logs`), not a path. So `resolve_file` takes the folder name, finds the matching folder in VS Code's recently opened list (`~/Documents/shadow-assistant/ai-logs`), and searches inside it for a single `test.txt`. Your file is `~/Desktop/test.txt`: you opened it in the `ai-logs` window, but it isn't inside that folder. The search finds nothing, so tier 2 is skipped.

**VS Code does know the real path.** It keeps per-window state in `~/.config/Code/User/workspaceStorage/<id>/state.vscdb`, and for your `ai-logs` window it lists:
- the open editors: `"path":"/home/juan/Desktop/test.txt"` (in `memento/workbench.parts.editor`)
- the editor history: `"resource":"file:///home/juan/Desktop/test.txt"` (in `history.entries`)

**Proposed fix:**
1. **Read that per-window state too.** `resolve_file` would find the window's state by its folder name (each workspace has a `workspace.json` naming its folder) and look for a file with the title's name:
   - First among the **open editors**, which is exact.
   - Then inside the folder, as today.
   - Then in that window's **editor history**.
   - If exactly one existing file matches, that's the path. If two different files with the same name match, it's still skipped, rather than guessing.
2. **Handle VS Code saving that state late.** As far as I know, VS Code writes this state periodically rather than the moment you open a file, possibly up to about a minute later. I'd verify the actual delay before relying on it. A file opened seconds before you start typing may not be listed yet when the session opens. So instead of giving up on the first try, `brain` would retry the lookup on each ingest pass, about once a second, while the session is open, for up to 2 minutes.
   - It takes the snapshot as soon as the file is found, but only if the file hasn't changed on disk since the session started. In that case the disk copy is still exactly what you started from.
   - If you saved before the lookup succeeded, it's skipped with a clear reason ("the file was saved before it could be identified"). It never replays from the wrong starting text.
3. **Clearer skip reasons:** `Untitled-1` would say `skipped: unsaved new file (nothing on disk to replay)` instead of "could not identify the file".
4. **Docs:** the README would recommend one VS Code setting that makes this instant and exact, a full path in the title:
   `"window.title": "${dirty}${activeEditorLong}${separator}${rootName}${separator}${appName}"`
   `resolve_file` already handles that form.

**Tests:**
- **Unit tests for `resolve_file`** against a fake VS Code config folder:
  - a file outside the workspace, found through the open editors;
  - one found through the editor history;
  - two different files with the same name, which must give "ambiguous";
  - an untitled file.
- **A session test** where the lookup fails at first and succeeds a few passes later, both with the file unchanged and with it saved in between.
- **The existing tier-2 end-to-end test**, extended with a file outside the workspace folder.

Should I go ahead?

content.content:
* **Sessions that changed nothing leave no row** (cursor movement only, a
  typo typed and deleted, whitespace).
* **VS Code tier 2 is opt-in** (`--vscode-replay`): it needs the file's
  content at session start (snapshot within 10 s, no unsaved changes),
  costs ~25 s for the first replay and ~1.2 GB while VS Code runs (capped,
  outside brain's budget), and runs with extensions disabled when your
  extensions exceed 300 MB. Suggestion acceptance may not replay the same.

  plain Ctrl+V does not paste in a terminal.
- **Tier 2, VS Code replayed in VS Code** (`reconstruct/vscode/`,
  `tier2.rs`, opt-in with `--vscode-replay`): when a VS Code session opens,
  the file is identified from the window title (an absolute path, or the
  default title resolved through VS Code's recently opened folders) and
  copied, unless it had unsaved changes or changed on disk after the session
  started. When the session closes with its tier 0/1 text, a worker replays
  the session's own keystrokes from the log into one warm, headless VS Code
  (Electron's headless mode, no display server) over the DevTools protocol on
  a pipe, in its own network namespace and a CPU/memory-capped systemd scope,
  with the user's settings and keybindings. It saves and the session's text
  becomes the changed lines. Failures and timeouts keep the tier 0/1 text;
  pending jobs survive restarts.

*Differs from the design*: no Xvfb (headless Electron needs no display), and
the CDP connection is a pipe, because the network namespace makes a TCP port
unreachable.
- **Other password prompts** are captured. AT-SPI's `password text` role
  would allow skipping them in apps that expose it.
- **VS Code tier 2** assumes the cursor starts at the end of the file,
  replays faster than a human (so accepting a suggestion may not replay the
  same), runs without extensions when they exceed 300 MB, and is the one part
  of `brain.db` a rebuild from the log does not reproduce (its file snapshot
  must be taken within 10 s of the session starting).
- **Desktop scope**: focus tracking needs KWin. On GNOME the equivalent would
  be a Shell extension; on wlroots compositors, `wlr-foreign-toplevel`. Keys
