(~/Desktop/test.txt in a window on the ai-logs folder): VS Code's
default title only has the file and folder names, and the lookup only
searched inside the folder.

The lookup now also reads VS Code's per-workspace state for that
folder: the editors the window has open (which records the full path
of every open file) and its editor history. The order is open editors,
then files under the folder, then the history; one existing match is
required, two different files of the same name stay ambiguous.

VS Code writes that state with a delay, so a file opened just before
typing may not be listed yet. Instead of giving up when the session
opens, the session is marked `resolving` and the lookup is retried on
each ingest step while it is open, for up to 2 minutes. A late
snapshot is still the starting text, since the file must not have
changed on disk since the session started; otherwise the session is
skipped with that reason. Unsaved new files (Untitled-1) are now
skipped as such instead of as "could not identify the file".

folder, history only, not listed yet, ambiguous, untitled), session

content.text:
Fixed and pushed (`337231c`, plus an `ai-logs/` refresh `eab169c`). The design is unchanged: VS Code sessions are still snapshotted while open, marked pending when they close, and replayed by the worker. What's new is how the edited file is found, plus a retry when it can't be found yet. Checked against your real VS Code config, your exact title (`test.txt - ai-logs - Visual Studio Code`) now resolves to `/home/juan/Desktop/test.txt`.

**What changed:**
- **The file lookup now reads VS Code's own state for that window** (per-workspace `state.vscdb`). It searches, in order:
  - The editors the window has open. This records the full path even for files outside the folder, which was your case.
  - Files under the folder, as before.
  - The window's editor history.
  - It needs exactly one existing match. Two different files with the same name are still skipped rather than guessed.
- **Retry while the session is open.** VS Code writes that state a little late, so if the file can't be found when the session opens, the session's `tier2_status` becomes `resolving`. `brain` tries again on each ingest pass, about once a second, for up to 2 minutes. A late snapshot is still correct, because it's only taken if the file hasn't changed on disk since the session started. If you saved before it was found, it's skipped and says so.
- **Clearer skip reasons:**
  - `Untitled-1` now gives `skipped: unsaved new file (nothing on disk to replay from)`.
  - A file saved too early gives `… changed on disk after the session started (saved before it could be snapshotted)`.
- **Testing support:** `VsCodeSnapshots::with_vscode_config(...)` lets a test supply a fake VS Code config.

**Tests:**
- **Lookup tests against a fake VS Code config:**
  - a file outside the folder, found through the open editors;
  - a file found only through the history;
  - a file not listed yet;
  - two open files with the same name, which stay ambiguous;
  - an open editor winning over a same-named file in the folder;
  - untitled titles.
- **Session test** with a fake snapshotter: found on the third try (`resolving` → `snapshot` → `pending`, and the job is queued); never found (skipped with the reason); found but not replayable (skipped and not asked again).
- **New end-to-end test with real VS Code:** a file in a separate "Desktop" folder that VS Code's state lists only after the session opened. `brain` finds it on a later pass, replays it, and marks it tier 2 `done`.
- **Results:** 127 unit tests, crash safety, `query_cli`, `perf_budget`, both tier-2 end-to-end tests and the real-config lookup test all pass. Clippy and the generated docs are clean.

**Docs:** the README and PLAN.md describe the lookup, the 2-minute retry and the skip reasons. The README also recommends one VS Code setting that makes it instant and exact, a full path in the title:
`"window.title": "${dirty}${activeEditorLong}${separator}${rootName}${separator}${appName}"`

**To try it yourself:**
```sh
make                                   # install the new build
./target/release/brain run --vscode-replay --data-dir /tmp/brain-manual
# open ~/Desktop/test.txt (saved) in your ai-logs VS Code window, type, then stop typing for 30+ s
sqlite3 /tmp/brain-manual/brain.db "SELECT id, tier_used, tier2_status, tier2_file FROM sessions WHERE app LIKE '%VSCode%'"
```
Expected: `tier2_status` goes `resolving` → `snapshot` → `pending` → `done`, with `tier_used = 2`. The first replay takes about 25 s while VS Code starts.

I've worked through everything in your data. Nothing is changed yet. Here's what happened, point by point.

## 1. Autocomplete (`st` → ↓↓↓↓ → Enter)
Your last C++ session logged: `⇥std::cout << st<Down><Down><Down><Down>⏎::endl;`
- **In your VS Code:** typing `st` opened the C++ extension's suggestion list (IntelliSense from `ms-vscode.cpptools`). Four Downs moved to `std` and Enter accepted it.
- **In the replay:** your extensions folder is **798 MB**, over the 300 MB copy limit, so the sandboxed VS Code ran **without the C++ extension**. There was no `std` suggestion to pick. The four Downs moved the cursor down four lines and Enter inserted a newline, which gave `std::cout << st\n\n\n\n ::endl;`.
- Even with extensions, picking a suggestion with arrow keys depends on what the language server offers at that exact moment. The replay types much faster than you, so it can't be made reliable. Tier 0/1 can't model suggestions at all.

## 2. "Doesn't take the current content after closing and reopening VS Code"
The replay *did* start from the file as it was on disk. The problem is **where the cursor starts**.

content.text:
Found it. **It isn't stuck in the database. DB Browser is showing an old snapshot.**

- **The data:** reading `/tmp/brain-manual/brain.db` now, the last session (49, `test.cpp`) is `closed`, ended by the idle timeout, with tier 2 `done`. The `brain run` you stopped also wrote its final `stop` event cleanly.
- **The lock:** DB Browser (pid 582603) still has the database open and holds a **read lock** on it. `/proc/locks` shows SQLite's shared lock on `brain.db` and a WAL read mark on `brain.db-shm`. That means DB Browser is inside an open read transaction.
- **Why that shows `open`:** SQLite gives a reader a frozen view of the database as of when its transaction began, and DB Browser keeps that transaction open, for example after an edit or a query in its Execute SQL tab. Its view is from a moment when session 49 was still open. F5 refreshes the table but stays in the same transaction, so you keep seeing `open`, even after `brain` closed it and stopped.
- **Side effect:** while that old view is held, SQLite can't fold its log back into the main file. That's why `brain.db-wal` has grown to 4 MB and `brain.db` was last updated at 15:50. It's harmless, and it clears when DB Browser lets go.

**To see the real state:** in DB Browser, use "Revert Changes" or close and reopen the database. Better, open it with **File → Open Database Read-Only**. Or use `brain query search …` or `sqlite3 /tmp/brain-manual/brain.db "SELECT id, status FROM sessions ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 5"`, neither of which holds a transaction open.

So nothing needs fixing in `brain` for this. I'll mention it in the README's "inspect the result" note: use a read-only connection, or the open session view will look stuck.

Next I'll implement the plan you approved: the saved-file text, the honest statuses, the test guards and the checks for leftovers.

249:* **Tier 2** (`--vscode-replay`): when a VS Code session closes, its
250-  keystrokes are replayed into a headless VS Code with your settings, in a
251-  network-less sandbox with capped CPU and memory. The session text then
252-  comes from VS Code itself (auto-indent, bracket pairs, your keybindings).
253-  The session stores the changed lines. If replay is impossible or fails,
254-  the tier 0/1 text stays, and the `tier2_status` column says why.
255-  The edited file is found from the window title: VS Code's default title
256-  only has the file and folder names, so `brain` looks the name up in VS
257-  Code's own state for that window (the editors it has open, also for files
258-  opened from outside the folder), under the folder, and in the window's
259-  editor history. VS Code records a newly opened file there a little late,
260-  so the lookup is retried while the session is open (up to 2 minutes).
261-  For an instant, exact match, put the full path in the title (VS Code
262-  setting `"window.title": "${dirty}${activeEditorLong}${separator}${rootName}${separator}${appName}"`).

because the sandbox runs without the user's 800 MB of extensions, and
edits made where VS Code had restored the cursor landed at the end of
the file. Meanwhile the user's VS Code had autosaved the exact result.

The worker now looks at the edited file first: if it was written after
the session's last keystroke (autosave, or Ctrl+S at the end), the
session text is the lines it changed from the initial content saved
when the session opened, with status `done: saved file`, and VS Code
is not started. Only otherwise does it replay, unchanged, with status
`done: replayed (best effort, unverified)` instead of plain `done`.

Tests no longer leave processes behind: every `brain run` they start
goes through a guard that stops it (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 s,
never signalling a reaped pid) even when the test fails, before its
temp directory is deleted, and each such test ends by checking that no
brain process still uses its data directory. A test run had left a
synthetic `brain run` typing into a deleted directory for 16 hours.
The tier 2 worker now also stops its VS Code instance when dropped.

A new test checks the saved-file path without VS Code (it runs with
`cargo test`); the replay tests expect the new status. The README
documents the statuses, and that a GUI holding a read transaction shows
closed sessions as `open`.

The VS Code fix is done and pushed (`4884e8d`), plus the README update `d9c5a78` and the `ai-logs/` refresh. Every test passes, and nothing is left running.

**Session text from the saved file**
- When a VS Code session closes, the worker first checks the edited file. If it was written **after your last keystroke** (your autosave, or Ctrl+S at the end), the session's text is the lines it changed from the initial content saved when the session opened. That's exactly what VS Code produced, including the `std` you picked from autocomplete and edits wherever the cursor really was.
- VS Code isn't started at all in that case.
- Only if the file wasn't saved after the last edit does the replay run, unchanged, as a best effort.
- The session still stores only the changed lines.

**Honest statuses**

| `tier2_status` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `done: saved file` | text from the file saved after the last edit; exact |
| `done: replayed (best effort, unverified)` | replay in VS Code; not checked against anything |
| `resolving` / `snapshot` / `pending` / `failed: …` / `skipped: …` | unchanged |

**Tests**
- **Guard against leftovers:** every `brain run` a test starts now goes through a guard. It stops the process even if the test fails partway: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 s, and it never signals a process that's already gone. The process stops before its temp folder is deleted. The tests that start one also check at the end that no `brain` process still uses their folder.
- **VS Code worker:** it now stops its VS Code instance when it goes out of scope.
- **New saved-file test:** it plays your C++ case: `st` + Down×4 + Enter, then an autosave. It must give `done: saved file` with exactly the changed line. It needs no VS Code, so it runs with plain `cargo test`.
- **Leftover check:** I checked the machine for anything my tests left behind. There are no stray processes, VS Code sandboxes, Kate windows, temp folders or systemd units. The only `brain run` is yours (pid 591827), and the one KWin script loaded is its focus tracker.
- **Results:** 127 unit tests, crash safety, `query_cli`, `perf_budget` and the saved-file test pass. The two replay end-to-end tests pass with real VS Code under their new status, and both Kate tests pass with the new guard. Clippy and the generated docs are clean.

**Docs**
- The README's tier-2 section explains saved file vs. replay, with the status table.
- "Inspect the result" now uses `sqlite3 -readonly` and explains the DB Browser stale-snapshot effect you ran into.
- PLAN.md and CLAUDE.md are updated (CLAUDE.md gains the test-guard rule).
- "Where the agent failed" now lists the overstated `done` status and the test that left a process running for 16 hours.

I've looked at your test and rethought the design. Nothing is changed yet.

## What I saw in your test (`/tmp/brain-manual2`)
- **Sessions 2 and 3 show `tier2_status = done`.** The build from my last change never writes plain `done`, so that run used an **older build**, probably the `/usr/bin/brain` from an earlier `make`. Their text (`\n\nstd `, `\   `) is the old replay output.
- **Session 1 was skipped:** `the file had unsaved changes when the session started`. VS Code still showed the unsaved dot when you started typing, so the file on disk wasn't the starting text.

The design you describe is better anyway: no replay at all.

## New design: the session's diff is its text
1. **When a VS Code session opens:** identify the file and save its content, exactly as today, including the window-state lookup and retries for files outside the folder.
2. **When the session closes,** check the file on disk right then, in the ingest thread with no worker:
   - **Saved during the session** (modified after it started): the session text is a **diff from the opening content to the saved content**, in git's style, with `-`/`+` lines and a hunk header per change:
     ```
     @@ -3 +3 @@
     -#include <stdio>
     +#include <iostream>
     @@ -15,0 +16,7 @@
     +int main() {
     +    int result = func(5);
     +    std::cout << "Result: " << result << std::endl;
     +    return 0;
     +}
     ```
     It shows what you did to the file in that session, whatever happened in VS Code (autocomplete, formatting, cursor jumps), with no replay.
   - **Not saved during the session:** no diff is possible, so the tier 0/1 text stays and the status says so.
3. **Honest statuses:**

| `tier2_status` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `resolving` / `snapshot` | finding the file / opening content saved (unchanged) |
| `done: diff of the saved file` | the file was saved after the last keystroke: the diff covers the whole session |
| `done: diff up to the last save` | saved during the session, but edits after the last save weren't saved, so they're not in the diff |
| `skipped: not saved during the session` | nothing to diff; tier 0/1 text kept |
| `skipped: unsaved new file` / `unsaved changes when the session started` / `could not identify the file…` | unchanged |

**One trade-off:** search covers the whole session text, so words on `-` lines (text you *deleted* in that session) will match that session too. They're visibly marked as removed.

## What gets removed
- **The whole replay:** `src/reconstruct/vscode/mod.rs` (the sandbox, VS Code launch, network namespace, systemd scope, idle shutdown, extension copying), `cdp.rs` and `keys.rs`. That's about 1,800 lines.
- **The background worker and its plumbing:**
  - in `tier2.rs`: `Tier2Worker`, `run_job`, `session_events` and the replay result types;
  - in `ingest.rs`: the result queue and job hand-off;
  - in `capture/mod.rs`: the worker thread;
  - the `pending` status and its job list in `sessions.rs`.
- **Tests:** `tests/vscode_replay.rs` (12 tests) goes. `tests/tier2_e2e.rs` is rewritten around saved-file diffs. These need no VS Code, so they run with plain `cargo test`.
- **Docs:** the README, PLAN.md and CLAUDE.md sections on replay, the sandbox, extensions and their costs.
- **VS Code no longer needs to be installed.** Only its config files are read, to identify the file.

**What stays:**
- the file lookup from titles and VS Code's window state (`vscode/title.rs`);
- the diff code (`vscode/diff.rs`), extended to produce the git-style format;
- the opening-content snapshots;
- the dirty and untitled checks.

## Two decisions for you
1. **Context lines:** git shows 3 unchanged lines around each change. I suggest **none** (`-U0`, as above): the session text is then only what changed, and search won't match untouched code. Or do you want git's 3 lines of context?
2. **The `--vscode-replay` flag:** with no replay, this costs almost nothing (a file copy and a diff). I suggest **removing the flag and always doing it** for VS Code. Or keep it opt-in, renamed to something like `--vscode-diff`?

# CLAUDE.md — instructions for coding agents working on `brain`

`brain` is a Rust CLI for the Endpoint "Shadow Assistant" home assignment
(`Endpoint Home Assignment.pdf`, not committed). One binary, two commands:
`brain run` captures keystrokes + focus and stores them; `brain query`
(`search`, `text`) answers questions while `run` keeps going.

Design doc (source of truth for architecture):
https://claude.ai/artifact/UTxCHmXHeSBaQASSNNiSP9 — `PLAN.md` is the in-repo
research/architecture write-up and must stay consistent with the code.

## Target platform

Ubuntu, **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Not GNOME. Keys come from evdev
(`/dev/input/event*`, user in the `input` group), resolved with libxkbcommon
(`libxkbcommon.so.0`, linked by file name, so no `-dev` package is needed).
Focus comes from a KWin script calling back over D-Bus. Tests that run by
default must not need hardware, a desktop or privileges: use
`brain run --synthetic RATE` (hidden flag) to drive the real pipeline. Only
the opt-in (`#[ignore]`) tests use `/dev/uinput`, Kate or VS Code.

## Hard requirements (from the assignment) — never regress these

- Capture is invisible: no input lag (we never grab devices), **≤ 1 % average
  CPU while typing, ≤ 32 MB RSS**, keeps working after sleep/wake.
- `kill -9` of `run` at any moment + restart ⇒ no corruption
  (`tests/crash_safety.rs` must stay green).
- `query` works while `run` writes and always sees a consistent state.
- Both commands take `--data-dir` (default `./brain-data`) and exit non-zero
  with a message on stderr on error. Query output is JSON on stdout, with
  times in local time (the log and database store UTC).

## Decisions already made by the owner — do not re-litigate

- `brain query text` reconstructs "stupidly": the keys typed in the time
  range, per app and window title, run through the tier 0/1 adapters from
  an empty text (no sessions involved); output `windows` + joined `text`.
  It replaced the earlier raw-keystroke output at the owner's request.
  Range: default last 10 min, `--at T` = the 10 minutes ending at T, or
  `--from/--to`. Times accept relative (`-2h`), local and RFC 3339 forms.
  `--app` may be part of the id; `text` resolves it to exactly one app and
  reports the full id.
- Sessions: keyed by (app, normalized window title); close after 30 s idle
  in that context or on Enter in single-line contexts; focus loss alone
  never closes a session; a title change of the typed window (a `renamed`
  focus event) shortly after a keystroke keeps the session.
- The mouse is not captured (owner's call): cursor moves made with the mouse
  are a documented limitation, not something to work around.
- Reconstruction tiers: 0 = generic buffer replay, 1 = per-app rules,
  2 = VS Code real-app replay, **opt-in** via `brain run --vscode-replay`,
  falling back to tier 0. Sessions, reconstruction and indexing are built
  before `brain query` (owner's call, changing the original stage order).
- Search is substring matching (FTS5 trigram, case- and accent-insensitive),
  not the design's porter stemming: `run` must find "rerun", `בית` "בבית".
- Sessions and their text must stay a pure function of the log: the crash
  test compares the live index with a fresh rebuild.
- Work went through stages (capture with sessions and indexing, query,
  end-to-end verification), each approved by the owner. Keep the habit for
  new work: build, run, test it yourself, report, then **stop and wait for
  explicit approval** before starting the next piece.

## Code map

```
src/main.rs              CLI (clap), error → stderr + exit 1
src/capture/mod.rs       `run` orchestration: sources, ingest thread, signals
src/capture/input.rs     poll loop over keyboards (evdev), hotplug, EVIOCSMASK
src/capture/keys.rs      pure key processing: xkb resolution + repeat synthesis
src/capture/xkb.rs       libxkbcommon FFI wrapper
src/capture/recorder.rs  stamps focus, appends to log, clipboard on paste, lock pause
src/capture/desktop.rs   D-Bus: KWin focus script, Klipper, lock, sleep, layouts
src/capture/synthetic.rs synthetic input source for tests/benchmarks
src/eventlog.rs          append-only JSONL log: torn-tail repair, line reader
src/store.rs             SQLite schema (WAL, FTS5), helpers
src/ingest.rs            log → SQLite, offset advanced in the same transaction
src/sessions.rs          session rules, open/close, live text, crash recovery
src/query.rs             `query search` / `query text`, time windows, JSON output
src/reconstruct/         buffer.rs tier 0 · apps.rs + editor.rs tier 1 ·
                         tier2.rs + vscode/ tier 2 (VS Code replay, opt-in)
src/event.rs, timefmt.rs event format, timestamp parsing/formatting
tests/                   integration tests that drive the real binary;
                         tests/common: uinput keyboard and KDE helpers
```

## Working rules

- **No backward compatibility.** This is the first robust version, still
  being built: change the log format, the schema or the CLI freely, with no
  migration, compatibility shims or legacy-format handling. Test data
  directories can be deleted and recreated.
- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` (zero warnings) and `cargo test`
  before every commit. Run `cargo test --release --test crash_safety` when
  touching the log, ingest or store.
- Keep the hot path (input thread) free of allocation-heavy work, blocking
  I/O other than the single log `write(2)`, and SQLite.
- The log is the ground truth; SQLite is derived and rebuildable. Never put
  data only in SQLite.
- Commit messages per https://cbea.ms/git-commit/ (imperative subject
  ≤ 50 chars, blank line, body wrapped at 72 explaining what and why).
  Commit at meaningful checkpoints.
- Prefer verifying behaviour by running the binary over reasoning about it;
  report exactly what was tested and what was not.
- Tests that need VS Code are `#[ignore]`: `cargo test --release --test
  vscode_replay --test tier2_e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1`.
- Every `brain run` a test starts goes through `tests/common::spawn_brain`
  (or `start_brain`): the guard stops it even when the test fails, and
  tests end with `assert_no_brain_on(data)`. No test may leave a process or
  a file behind.
- `tests/repeat_e2e.rs` and `tests/real_keyboard_e2e.rs` (`#[ignore]`) type
  into real Kate windows through /dev/uinput: they need an unlocked KDE
  session, `scripts/setup-test-permissions.sh`, and nobody touching the
  keyboard or mouse while they run. They only type while brain's log shows
  the intended window focused.
- The input loop must deliver key transitions before emitting the repeats
  due at the same time (`keys::tests::ticking_past_an_unread_release_adds_repeats`).
- Never change desktop session state you did not set up (lock/unlock,
  suspend); check it first and restore it.

- [brain assignment decisions](brain-assignment-decisions.md) — user-confirmed choices: raw `query text`, stage gates, opt-in VS Code tier 2, private repo; KDE Wayland machine
- [Check lock state before lock tests](check-lock-before-lock-tests.md) — never unlock-session a screen found locked; restore desktop state after tests

33	    let status = std::fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{pid}/status")).unwrap();

# PDF Processing Guide

## Overview

This guide covers essential PDF processing operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features, JavaScript libraries, and detailed examples, see REFERENCE.md. If you need to fill out a PDF form, read FORMS.md and follow its instructions.

## Quick Start

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Read a PDF
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
print(f"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}")

# Extract text
text = ""
for page in reader.pages:
    text += page.extract_text()
```

## Python Libraries

### pypdf - Basic Operations

#### Merge PDFs
```python
from pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader

writer = PdfWriter()
for pdf_file in ["doc1.pdf", "doc2.pdf", "doc3.pdf"]:
    reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)
    for page in reader.pages:
        writer.add_page(page)

with open("merged.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

#### Split PDF
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
    writer = PdfWriter()
    writer.add_page(page)
    with open(f"page_{i+1}.pdf", "wb") as output:
        writer.write(output)
```

#### Extract Metadata
```python
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
meta = reader.metadata
print(f"Title: {meta.title}")
print(f"Author: {meta.author}")
print(f"Subject: {meta.subject}")
print(f"Creator: {meta.creator}")
```

#### Rotate Pages
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

page = reader.pages[0]
page.rotate(90)  # Rotate 90 degrees clockwise
writer.add_page(page)

with open("rotated.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### pdfplumber - Text and Table Extraction

#### Extract Text with Layout
```python
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for page in pdf.pages:
        text = page.extract_text()
        print(text)
```

#### Extract Tables
```python
with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for j, table in enumerate(tables):
            print(f"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:")
            for row in table:
                print(row)
```

#### Advanced Table Extraction
```python
import pandas as pd

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    all_tables = []
    for page in pdf.pages:
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for table in tables:
            if table:  # Check if table is not empty
                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])
                all_tables.append(df)

# Combine all tables
if all_tables:
    combined_df = pd.concat(all_tables, ignore_index=True)
    combined_df.to_excel("extracted_tables.xlsx", index=False)
```

### reportlab - Create PDFs

#### Basic PDF Creation
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

c = canvas.Canvas("hello.pdf", pagesize=letter)
width, height = letter

# Add text
c.drawString(100, height - 100, "Hello World!")
c.drawString(100, height - 120, "This is a PDF created with reportlab")

# Add a line
c.line(100, height - 140, 400, height - 140)

# Save
c.save()
```

#### Create PDF with Multiple Pages
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, PageBreak
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

doc = SimpleDocTemplate("report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
story = []

# Add content
title = Paragraph("Report Title", styles['Title'])
story.append(title)
story.append(Spacer(1, 12))

body = Paragraph("This is the body of the report. " * 20, styles['Normal'])
story.append(body)
story.append(PageBreak())

# Page 2
story.append(Paragraph("Page 2", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph("Content for page 2", styles['Normal']))

# Build PDF
doc.build(story)
```

#### Subscripts and Superscripts

**IMPORTANT**: Never use Unicode subscript/superscript characters (₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉, ⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹) in ReportLab PDFs. The built-in fonts do not include these glyphs, causing them to render as solid black boxes.

Instead, use ReportLab's XML markup tags in Paragraph objects:
```python
from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

# Subscripts: use <sub> tag
chemical = Paragraph("H<sub>2</sub>O", styles['Normal'])

# Superscripts: use <super> tag
squared = Paragraph("x<super>2</super> + y<super>2</super>", styles['Normal'])
```

For canvas-drawn text (not Paragraph objects), manually adjust font the size and position rather than using Unicode subscripts/superscripts.

## Command-Line Tools

### pdftotext (poppler-utils)
```bash
# Extract text
pdftotext input.pdf output.txt

# Extract text preserving layout
pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt

# Extract specific pages
pdftotext -f 1 -l 5 input.pdf output.txt  # Pages 1-5
```

### qpdf
```bash
# Merge PDFs
qpdf --empty --pages file1.pdf file2.pdf -- merged.pdf

# Split pages
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- pages1-5.pdf
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 6-10 -- pages6-10.pdf

# Rotate pages
qpdf input.pdf output.pdf --rotate=+90:1  # Rotate page 1 by 90 degrees

# Remove password
qpdf --password=mypassword --decrypt encrypted.pdf decrypted.pdf
```

### pdftk (if available)
```bash
# Merge
pdftk file1.pdf file2.pdf cat output merged.pdf

# Split
pdftk input.pdf burst

# Rotate
pdftk input.pdf rotate 1east output rotated.pdf
```

## Common Tasks

### Extract Text from Scanned PDFs
```python
# Requires: pip install pytesseract pdf2image
import pytesseract
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

# Convert PDF to images
images = convert_from_path('scanned.pdf')

# OCR each page
text = ""
for i, image in enumerate(images):
    text += f"Page {i+1}:\n"
    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(image)
    text += "\n\n"

print(text)
```

### Add Watermark
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Create watermark (or load existing)
watermark = PdfReader("watermark.pdf").pages[0]

# Apply to all pages
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    page.merge_page(watermark)
    writer.add_page(page)

with open("watermarked.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### Extract Images
```bash
# Using pdfimages (poppler-utils)
pdfimages -j input.pdf output_prefix

# This extracts all images as output_prefix-000.jpg, output_prefix-001.jpg, etc.
```

### Password Protection
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    writer.add_page(page)

# Add password
writer.encrypt("userpassword", "ownerpassword")

with open("encrypted.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

## Quick Reference

| Task | Best Tool | Command/Code |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| Merge PDFs | pypdf | `writer.add_page(page)` |
| Split PDFs | pypdf | One page per file |
| Extract text | pdfplumber | `page.extract_text()` |
| Extract tables | pdfplumber | `page.extract_tables()` |
| Create PDFs | reportlab | Canvas or Platypus |
| Command line merge | qpdf | `qpdf --empty --pages ...` |
| OCR scanned PDFs | pytesseract | Convert to image first |
| Fill PDF forms | pdf-lib or pypdf (see FORMS.md) | See FORMS.md |

## Next Steps

- For advanced pypdfium2 usage, see REFERENCE.md
- For JavaScript libraries (pdf-lib), see REFERENCE.md
- If you need to fill out a PDF form, follow the instructions in FORMS.md
- For troubleshooting guides, see REFERENCE.md

# PDF Processing Guide

## Overview

This guide covers essential PDF processing operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features, JavaScript libraries, and detailed examples, see REFERENCE.md. If you need to fill out a PDF form, read FORMS.md and follow its instructions.

## Quick Start

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Read a PDF
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
print(f"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}")

# Extract text
text = ""
for page in reader.pages:
    text += page.extract_text()
```

## Python Libraries

### pypdf - Basic Operations

#### Merge PDFs
```python
from pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader

writer = PdfWriter()
for pdf_file in ["doc1.pdf", "doc2.pdf", "doc3.pdf"]:
    reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)
    for page in reader.pages:
        writer.add_page(page)

with open("merged.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

#### Split PDF
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
    writer = PdfWriter()
    writer.add_page(page)
    with open(f"page_{i+1}.pdf", "wb") as output:
        writer.write(output)
```

#### Extract Metadata
```python
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
meta = reader.metadata
print(f"Title: {meta.title}")
print(f"Author: {meta.author}")
print(f"Subject: {meta.subject}")
print(f"Creator: {meta.creator}")
```

#### Rotate Pages
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

page = reader.pages[0]
page.rotate(90)  # Rotate 90 degrees clockwise
writer.add_page(page)

with open("rotated.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### pdfplumber - Text and Table Extraction

#### Extract Text with Layout
```python
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for page in pdf.pages:
        text = page.extract_text()
        print(text)
```

#### Extract Tables
```python
with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for j, table in enumerate(tables):
            print(f"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:")
            for row in table:
                print(row)
```

#### Advanced Table Extraction
```python
import pandas as pd

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    all_tables = []
    for page in pdf.pages:
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for table in tables:
            if table:  # Check if table is not empty
                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])
                all_tables.append(df)

# Combine all tables
if all_tables:
    combined_df = pd.concat(all_tables, ignore_index=True)
    combined_df.to_excel("extracted_tables.xlsx", index=False)
```

### reportlab - Create PDFs

#### Basic PDF Creation
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

c = canvas.Canvas("hello.pdf", pagesize=letter)
width, height = letter

# Add text
c.drawString(100, height - 100, "Hello World!")
c.drawString(100, height - 120, "This is a PDF created with reportlab")

# Add a line
c.line(100, height - 140, 400, height - 140)

# Save
c.save()
```

#### Create PDF with Multiple Pages
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, PageBreak
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

doc = SimpleDocTemplate("report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
story = []

# Add content
title = Paragraph("Report Title", styles['Title'])
story.append(title)
story.append(Spacer(1, 12))

body = Paragraph("This is the body of the report. " * 20, styles['Normal'])
story.append(body)
story.append(PageBreak())

# Page 2
story.append(Paragraph("Page 2", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph("Content for page 2", styles['Normal']))

# Build PDF
doc.build(story)
```

#### Subscripts and Superscripts

**IMPORTANT**: Never use Unicode subscript/superscript characters (₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉, ⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹) in ReportLab PDFs. The built-in fonts do not include these glyphs, causing them to render as solid black boxes.

Instead, use ReportLab's XML markup tags in Paragraph objects:
```python
from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

# Subscripts: use <sub> tag
chemical = Paragraph("H<sub>2</sub>O", styles['Normal'])

# Superscripts: use <super> tag
squared = Paragraph("x<super>2</super> + y<super>2</super>", styles['Normal'])
```

For canvas-drawn text (not Paragraph objects), manually adjust font the size and position rather than using Unicode subscripts/superscripts.

## Command-Line Tools

### pdftotext (poppler-utils)
```bash
# Extract text
pdftotext input.pdf output.txt

# Extract text preserving layout
pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt

# Extract specific pages
pdftotext -f 1 -l 5 input.pdf output.txt  # Pages 1-5
```

### qpdf
```bash
# Merge PDFs
qpdf --empty --pages file1.pdf file2.pdf -- merged.pdf

# Split pages
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- pages1-5.pdf
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 6-10 -- pages6-10.pdf

# Rotate pages
qpdf input.pdf output.pdf --rotate=+90:1  # Rotate page 1 by 90 degrees

# Remove password
qpdf --password=mypassword --decrypt encrypted.pdf decrypted.pdf
```

### pdftk (if available)
```bash
# Merge
pdftk file1.pdf file2.pdf cat output merged.pdf

# Split
pdftk input.pdf burst

# Rotate
pdftk input.pdf rotate 1east output rotated.pdf
```

## Common Tasks

### Extract Text from Scanned PDFs
```python
# Requires: pip install pytesseract pdf2image
import pytesseract
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

# Convert PDF to images
images = convert_from_path('scanned.pdf')

# OCR each page
text = ""
for i, image in enumerate(images):
    text += f"Page {i+1}:\n"
    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(image)
    text += "\n\n"

print(text)
```

### Add Watermark
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Create watermark (or load existing)
watermark = PdfReader("watermark.pdf").pages[0]

# Apply to all pages
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    page.merge_page(watermark)
    writer.add_page(page)

with open("watermarked.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### Extract Images
```bash
# Using pdfimages (poppler-utils)
pdfimages -j input.pdf output_prefix

# This extracts all images as output_prefix-000.jpg, output_prefix-001.jpg, etc.
```

### Password Protection
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    writer.add_page(page)

# Add password
writer.encrypt("userpassword", "ownerpassword")

with open("encrypted.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

## Quick Reference

| Task | Best Tool | Command/Code |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| Merge PDFs | pypdf | `writer.add_page(page)` |
| Split PDFs | pypdf | One page per file |
| Extract text | pdfplumber | `page.extract_text()` |
| Extract tables | pdfplumber | `page.extract_tables()` |
| Create PDFs | reportlab | Canvas or Platypus |
| Command line merge | qpdf | `qpdf --empty --pages ...` |
| OCR scanned PDFs | pytesseract | Convert to image first |
| Fill PDF forms | pdf-lib or pypdf (see FORMS.md) | See FORMS.md |

## Next Steps

- For advanced pypdfium2 usage, see REFERENCE.md
- For JavaScript libraries (pdf-lib), see REFERENCE.md
- If you need to fill out a PDF form, follow the instructions in FORMS.md
- For troubleshooting guides, see REFERENCE.md

definition.name: EnterWorktree
definition.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

name.description: Optional name for a new worktree. Each "/"-separated segment may contain only letters, digits, dots, underscores, and dashes; max 64 chars total. A random name is generated if not provided. Mutually exclusive with `path`.

path.description: Path to an existing worktree to switch into instead of creating a new one. Must appear in `git worktree list` for the current repo — or, on first entry from the launch directory, for a repo nested inside it (multi-repo workspace). Mutually exclusive with `name`.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". - code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option. - Use the max or ultra level only when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask for one, never on your own judgment: they are the costliest reviews and start many reviewer subagents.

Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.
