182	## 3. Event format and ingestion
183	
184	### 3.1 The capture log
185	
186	`events.jsonl`, one JSON object per line, in the assignment's format plus the
187	window title:
188	
189	```json
190	{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:37:56.937Z","app":"org.kde.kate","type":"key","key":"H","mods":["shift"],"window":"notes.md — Kate"}
191	{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:37:57.132Z","app":"org.kde.kate","type":"key","key":"Backspace","mods":[],"repeat":true,"window":"notes.md — Kate"}
192	{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:38:00.003Z","app":"google-chrome","type":"focus","window":"New tab - Google Chrome"}
193	{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:38:01.120Z","app":"google-chrome","type":"focus","window":"brain - Google Search - Google Chrome","renamed":true}
194	{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:38:02.410Z","app":"google-chrome","type":"paste","text":"pasted words","window":"New tab - Google Chrome"}
195	{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:36:48.298Z","app":"org.kde.kate","type":"system","state":"sleep"}
196	```
197	
198	Types: `key` (with `repeat: true` for synthesized repeats), `focus` (a
199	window activated, or with `renamed: true` the active window's title
200	changed), `paste`, and `system` (`start`, `stop`,
201	`sleep`, `wake`, `lock`, `unlock`). Timestamps are RFC 3339 UTC with
202	milliseconds: fixed width, so they sort as strings.
203	
204	### 3.2 Write path
205	
206	- One `write(2)` per event, of a complete line, from the input thread (or a
207	  D-Bus thread for focus, lock and sleep events) under one mutex. The event
208	  is in the kernel's page cache when the call returns, so a crash of brain
209	  loses nothing; a power loss can lose the last second.
210	- `fdatasync` at most once per second, from the ingest thread, only if
211	  something was written.
212	- On open, a torn last line (a `kill -9` or power loss mid-write) is cut off;
213	  readers only ever return complete lines.
214	
215	### 3.3 Ingest
216	
217	Once a second, the ingest thread syncs the log and runs steps of at most 5,000
218	lines until it has caught up. **Each step is one SQLite transaction** that
219	holds everything derived from those lines and the new log offset:
220	
221	1. read complete lines from `ingest_state.log_offset`;
222	2. write a log checkpoint at most every 5 s of log time;
223	3. feed each event to the session engine (section 4);
224	4. once caught up, close sessions idle on the wall clock, write finished tier
225	   2 results, refresh the live text of open sessions;
226	5. store the new offset and commit.
227	
228	If the commit fails nothing is visible and the same lines are read again; the
229	in-memory session state is rebuilt from the database first, so it cannot run
230	ahead. After the commit, tier 2 jobs are handed to the worker.
231	
232	**Why a thread in the same process**: one binary and one lock on the data
233	directory, no IPC, and ingest can never run without capture or vice versa.
234	The capture path never touches SQLite, so a slow transaction cannot delay
235	reading the keyboard.
236	
237	**Why not write keystrokes to SQLite directly**: a SQLite write can stall
238	(WAL checkpoints, FTS updates, lock contention), and a stalled reader of the
239	keyboard overflows the kernel's small buffer and loses keys. The append-only
240	log also makes the database disposable: a schema change, or a bug in session
241	logic, is fixed by deleting `brain.db`, which is rebuilt from the log.
242	
243	### 3.4 `kill -9` at each point
244	
245	| Killed while... | After restart |
246	|---|---|
247	| writing a log line | the torn line is cut off; everything before it is intact |
248	| between a write and the next ingest | ingest resumes from its offset and reads the new lines |
249	| inside an ingest transaction | SQLite rolls it back; the offset still points before those lines, so they are read again: no gap, no duplicate |
250	| with sessions open | open sessions are rebuilt from the database and their events replayed from the log (section 4.5); the restart's `start` event then closes them |
251	
252	`tests/crash_safety.rs` kills brain 25 times under load and checks database
253	integrity, offsets on line boundaries, a complete log, and that every session,
254	document and checkpoint equals a clean rebuild from the log.
255	
256	## 4. Sessions and reconstruction
257	
258	(`src/sessions.rs`, `src/reconstruct/`)
259	
260	### 4.1 Definition
261	
262	- A session is one **`(app, window title)`**. The title is normalized first:
263	  leading status glyphs are removed (an editor's unsaved-file dot, the
264	  spinners terminal programs animate in titles) and so are `*` / `[modified]`
265	  markers, because they change while typing.
266	- **Titles renamed by the typing itself** keep the session: VS Code names a
267	  new file after its first line, a mail window after its subject. A title
268	  change *of the same window* (a `renamed` focus event) within 1 s of a
269	  keystroke in it, with no shortcut in between (Ctrl+Tab, Alt+Tab may switch
270	  tabs or windows), makes the new title an alias of the open session. A
271	  window activation, by keyboard or mouse, ends any possible rename.
272	- A session **closes** after **30 s without activity in that window**, or at
273	  once when a single-line field commits (Enter at a shell prompt, in a chat
274	  box, an address bar or a launcher), is cancelled (Ctrl+C at a prompt), or
275	  is left for another field of the same window (Tab, Ctrl+L/K/T/W in a
276	  browser), and when `brain run` stops or restarts.
277	- **Focus loss alone never closes a session**: switching away and back
278	  within 30 s of that window's last keystroke resumes it.
279	- Shortcuts with no modelled effect (Ctrl+C copy, Alt+Tab, Ctrl+S, F-keys)
280	  are not activity: they neither open nor extend a session.
281	- A session that changed nothing (cursor movement only, a typo typed and
282	  deleted, whitespace) leaves no row; a committed non-empty line always
283	  does (a shell command run again from history).
284	- **Idle closing on the clock** happens only once ingest has caught up with
285	  the log, and 2 s past the 30 s timeout, so it always agrees with the same
286	  rule applied to event times on a rebuild.
287	
288	### 4.2 Text across sessions
289	
290	Editors and unknown (multi-line) apps keep a **document per window** between
291	sessions (`context_state`, forgotten after 24 h), so the next session
292	continues where the previous one left it, cursor included. A session's text
293	is that document when the session closes: a word present at close stays
294	findable through that session even if a later session deletes it.
295	Single-line fields (terminals, browsers, chat, launchers) start every session
296	empty: their titles are reused by unrelated fields ("New tab", "~"), so
297	carrying text over would mix them.
298	
299	### 4.3 The engine: incremental, in memory, from the log
300	
301	Ingest keeps one entry per open session in memory: its row id, a text buffer
302	(the reconstruction so far, with cursor, selection and undo history), and its
303	last activity. Each logged event is routed by its own `(app, window)` to its
304	session and applied once, the moment ingest reads it; switching between apps
305	is just a different map entry. The log interleaves apps, but filtering it per
306	key preserves each window's order. Every ingest step writes the current text
307	of changed open sessions, so `search` sees what is being typed now. Closing a
308	session writes the text it already has.
309	
310	*Differs from the design*, which reconstructed each session at close and
311	rebuilt open sessions just in time for live search. The result is the same;
312	incremental work costs a constant amount per key instead of growing with the
313	session.
314	
315	### 4.4 Reconstruction tiers
316	
317	- **Tier 0, a generic text field** (`reconstruct/buffer.rs`): insertion
318	  replacing the selection, Backspace/Delete (word-wise with Ctrl), arrows,
319	  Home/End, Up/Down keeping the column, PageUp/PageDown, Shift-selection,
320	  select-all, cut, and undo/redo grouped about a word at a time. A 200,000
321	  character cap per buffer keeps memory bounded. An unknown cursor position
322	  is assumed to be at the end.
323	- **Tier 1, per-app rules** (`reconstruct/apps.rs`, `editor.rs`): a small
324	  table classifies app ids into terminal, browser, chat, launcher, editor or
325	  generic. It decides whether Enter commits or inserts a newline (Shift+Enter
326	  is a newline in browsers and chat), readline editing in terminals
327	  (Ctrl+A/E/U/K/W, Alt+B/F) and history recall with Up/Down from the commands
328	  brain saw committed in that terminal app, browser field changes, and that
329	  plain Ctrl+V does not paste in a terminal.
330	- **Tier 2, VS Code replayed in VS Code** (`reconstruct/vscode/`,
331	  `tier2.rs`, opt-in with `--vscode-replay`): when a VS Code session opens,
332	  the file is identified from the window title: an absolute path if the
333	  title has one, otherwise the title's file name looked up in VS Code's
334	  per-workspace state for the window's folder (its open editors, which also
335	  covers files opened from outside the folder), under that folder, then in
336	  the window's editor history; one existing match is required. VS Code
337	  writes that state with a delay, so an unidentified file is looked up
338	  again on each ingest step while the session is open, for up to 2 minutes.
339	  The file is copied, unless it is an unsaved new file (`Untitled-1`), had
340	  unsaved changes when the session started, or changed on disk after the
341	  session started (a late snapshot is therefore still the starting text).
342	  When the session closes with its tier 0/1 text, a worker works out its
343	  real text. If the file on disk was written after the session's last
344	  keystroke (autosave, or Ctrl+S at the end), it already holds what VS Code
345	  made of the keys: the session's text is a git-style unified diff from the
346	  snapshot to the saved file, 3 lines of context (`done: saved file`,
347	  exact, VS Code not started; Myers line diff with git's "slide down"
348	  placement of ambiguous runs). Otherwise the
349	  worker replays the session's own keystrokes from the log into one warm,
350	  headless VS Code (Electron's headless mode, no display server) over the
351	  DevTools protocol on a pipe, in its own network namespace and a
352	  CPU/memory-capped systemd scope, with the user's settings and keybindings,
353	  saves, and takes the changed lines (`done: replayed (best effort,
354	  unverified)`: cursor assumed at the end, no extensions above 300 MB, so
355	  extension autocomplete is not reproduced). Failures and timeouts keep the
356	  tier 0/1 text; pending jobs survive restarts.
357	
358	  With tier 2 on, every VS Code key except desktop (Super) shortcuts opens
359	  or extends the session, even ones tier 0/1 ignores (Ctrl+D, Alt+Up,
360	  Ctrl+S), and a session with a snapshot is kept at close even if its tier
361	  0/1 text is unchanged (`pending: saved file only`): it gets the saved
362	  file's diff, or is removed when the file was not saved after it; any
363	  session whose saved diff is empty is removed too. Because the snapshot is
364	  taken when ingest opens the session (up to 1 s after the first key), a
365	  focus change to VS Code wakes the ingest thread at once and the file is
366	  copied on focus; a session that starts within 10 s and finds its file
367	  saved before its own snapshot uses that copy, if the file was not
368	  modified after the session started.
369	
370	*Differs from the design*: no Xvfb (headless Electron needs no display), and
371	the CDP connection is a pipe, because the network namespace makes a TCP port
372	unreachable.
373	
374	### 4.5 Restart with open sessions
375	
376	On start, ingest loads the sessions still open in the database, restores
377	their starting documents from `context_state`, and replays their events from
378	each session's `start_offset` up to the ingested offset, through the same
379	key-to-action rules. The `start` event that follows closes them (input while
380	brain was not running is unknown). Everything the engine decides is a
381	function of the log, so a database rebuilt from the log alone is identical;
382	`sessions::tests::crash_recovery_reproduces_an_uninterrupted_run` restarts
383	ingest after every line to prove it.
384	
385	## 5. Storage and indexing
386	
387	### 5.1 Layout
388	
389	| Path | What |
390	|---|---|
391	| `events.jsonl` | the capture log (0600), ground truth |
392	| `brain.db` (+ `-wal`, `-shm`) | SQLite index, derived |
393	| `run.lock` | flock held by the running `brain run` |
394	| `kwin/` | the generated KWin script |
395	| `vscode/` | tier 2 sandbox and file snapshots |
396	
397	The directory is created 0700 and brain runs with umask 077.
398	
399	### 5.2 Schema (version 4)
400	
401	- **`sessions`**: `id`, `app`, `window` (normalized), `started_at`,
402	  `ended_at` (NULL while open), `status`, `tier_used`, `reconstructed_text`,
403	  `start_offset` / `end_offset` (the session's events in the log),
404	  `end_reason` (`idle`, `commit`, `cancel`, `field`, `stop`, `restart`),
405	  `tier2_status`, `tier2_file`. Indexes on `(app, started_at)`, `status`, and
406	  `(app, end_reason, end_offset)` for shell history.
407	- **`sessions_fts`**: FTS5 over `reconstructed_text`, external content (the
408	  text is stored once, in `sessions`), kept in sync by insert/update/delete
409	  triggers in the same transaction.
410	- **`context_state`**: each multi-line window's document between sessions.
411	- **`ingest_state`**: the single log offset.
412	- **`log_checkpoints`**: `(ts, byte_offset)`, at most one per 5 s of log time.
413	
414	There are no migrations (first version): a database from another schema
415	version is refused with a message to delete it.
416	
417	### 5.3 Why SQLite, WAL and FTS5
418	
419	- **WAL**: one writer (ingest) never blocks readers, and each `brain query`
420	  sees a snapshot as of the start of its read: never a half-written session.
421	- **`synchronous = NORMAL`**: no fsync per commit. A power loss can drop the
422	  last commits but never corrupts the database, and the dropped work is
423	  re-derived from the log because the offset rolls back with it.
424	- **FTS5** is in SQLite itself (bundled, no server), and external content
425	  avoids storing session text twice.
426	- A 1 MiB page cache keeps the writer inside the memory budget.
427	
428	### 5.4 Tokenizer: trigram
429	
430	The index uses FTS5's **trigram** tokenizer, case- and accent-insensitive: a
431	query word matches anywhere inside a word (`run` finds "rerun", `cafe` finds
432	"Café"). *Differs from the design* (porter stemming), on the owner's call:
433	search should behave as "contains", and porter is English-only, while
434	trigram finds Hebrew words with attached prefixes (`בית` in "בבית"). Words
435	shorter than 3 characters cannot use the trigram index and are matched with
436	`LIKE`.
437	
438	### 5.5 Log checkpoints
439	
440	`query text` must read the keys of a time window from the log without
441	scanning it from the start. Each checkpoint says "the event at this byte has
442	this timestamp". Because the log is written in time order, starting at the
443	latest checkpoint at or before the window misses nothing, and reads at most
444	5 s of log before the window; reading stops 60 s of log after it. Per-app
445	checkpoints would not save work, since the log interleaves apps and the
446	window has to be read anyway. Clock steps backwards are discussed in section
447	10.
448	
449	## 6. Query semantics
450	
451	(`src/query.rs`)
452	
453	- **`brain query search "<words>" [--app A] [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]
454	  [--limit N]`**: sessions whose text contains every word (substrings, any
455	  case), newest first, default limit 20, with a snippet around the first
456	  match. Open sessions are included with their live text and
457	  `ended_at: null`. A session is in a time window if it overlaps it.
458	- **`brain query text --app A [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]`**: what was typed
459	  into the app during the time range, reconstructed. The range's key and
460	  paste events (read from the log, section 5.5) are split per app window
461	  (window title) and each app window's events run, from an empty text,
462	  through the app's tier 0/1 adapter: the same `editor::action` and
463	  `FieldEditor` the session engine uses, without sessions. A submit in a
464	  single-line field (Enter at a shell prompt) keeps the line and continues
465	  on a fresh one; Up recalls lines submitted earlier in the same app window.
466	  Output: `windows` (each app window's text, by first keystroke) and `text`
467	  (them joined, one per line). *Differs from the design*, where `text` was
468	  the raw keystroke stream; the owner changed it.
469	- **`--app A`** can be part of an app id, ignoring case. `search` keeps
470	  every matching app; `text` resolves it to one full id (exact match first,
471	  else the single id containing it; ambiguous or unknown is an error) and
472	  reports that id.
473	- **Windows**: `--at T` is the 10 minutes ending at T; `--from` alone runs to
474	  now; `--from` and `--to` together are explicit; `--to` alone is the 10
475	  minutes ending at T for `text` and everything up to T for `search`; no
476	  flags means the last 10 minutes for `text` and all time for `search`.
477	- **Times**: relative (`-30s`, `-15m`, `-2h`, `-1d`, `-1h30m`, `now`), local
478	  (`2026-11-16 14:00`, a date, or a time of day meaning today; DST folds
479	  take the earlier instant, DST gaps are an error), or RFC 3339 with a zone.
480	  Output times are local with their offset (RFC 3339), and the resolved
481	  window is echoed; the log and the database store UTC.
482	- Errors (empty query, bad time, empty window, `--at` with `--from`/`--to`,
483	  missing data directory) go to stderr with a non-zero exit code.
484	
485	## 7. Resource budget
486	
487	- **No input lag by construction**: brain is a passive reader, not on the
488	  delivery path. Even a completely stalled brain cannot delay a keystroke.
489	- **CPU**: no async runtime and no polling. The input thread sleeps in
490	  `poll` and wakes per key event (and per repeat while a key is held); one
491	  `write` per event; one small transaction per second; SQLite work per
492	  session proportional to its text.
493	- **Memory**: few threads with small stacks, a 1 MiB SQLite cache, a capped
494	  buffer per open session (usually one to three are open), no copy of closed
495	  sessions in memory.
496	- **Measured** (`tests/perf_budget.rs`, part of `cargo test`): 8 keys/s for
497	  30 s through the whole pipeline with a query every 3 s: **0.1 % CPU, 8.1 MB
498	  peak RSS**. A real run idles at about 8 MB.
499	- The opt-in VS Code instance runs outside brain's budget, in its own
500	  systemd scope capped at 50 % CPU and 1.5 GB, shut down after 10 minutes
501	  idle.
502	
503	## 8. Security and privacy
504	
505	- **Local only.** No network code in brain; the VS Code replay instance runs
506	  in a network namespace with only loopback.
507	- **Data at rest**: directory 0700, files 0600.
508	- **Privilege**: brain runs as the user, as a systemd *user* service if
509	  wanted (`make install-service`), never as root. The service's data is its
510	  systemd state directory (`~/.local/state/brain`, mode 0700), deleted by
511	  `make uninstall-service` unless `KEEP_DATA=1`. Reading keyboards needs
512	  the `input` group, which lets any process of the user read all keyboards;
513	  the README states this trade-off.
514	- **Passwords**: capture pauses while the screen is locked. Other password
515	  prompts (sudo in a terminal, web logins) cannot be told apart from typing
516	  by key events alone (section 10).
517	- **Clipboard**: read only on a paste shortcut.
518	- **KWin integration** only reads window metadata and calls one D-Bus
519	  method; calls not coming from KWin are ignored.
520	- **Queries**: search words are quoted for FTS5 and all SQL uses bound
521	  parameters.
522	- **Tests that need privileges** get exactly two narrow ones
523	  (`scripts/setup-test-permissions.sh`): passwordless `rtcwake -m no -s 30`
524	  only, and `/dev/uinput` for the user at the local seat.
525	
526	## 9. Testing strategy
527	
528	- **Unit tests** (about 120, `cargo test`): key resolution and layouts,
529	  repeat synthesis (including a 300-scenario stress test against an
530	  independent model, with random early and late wakeups), the recorder, the
531	  log's torn-tail repair, schema and search, ingest, the tier 0 buffer and
532	  tier 1 rules, title normalization and renames, every session rule, crash
533	  recovery after every line, time parsing, query windows, and `query text`'s
534	  per-window reconstruction (the README's example, event for event).
535	- **Integration tests run by default**: `crash_safety` (25 `kill -9`s under
536	  load, compared with a clean rebuild), `query_cli` (the binary's JSON
537	  output, search semantics through the CLI, time windows, reconstructed
538	  text including the README's example, errors, and thousands of queries
539	  while `run` writes), `perf_budget` (CPU and
540	  memory budget).
541	- **Opt-in tests against real software**: `repeat_e2e` and
542	  `real_keyboard_e2e` type through a uinput keyboard into real Kate windows
543	  and compare Kate's saved files with brain (held-key repeats, Hebrew via
544	  Alt+Shift, focus moving between windows, keyboard unplug/replug);
545	  `vscode_replay` and `tier2_e2e` drive real VS Code.
546	- **Manual, once**: sleep/wake through a real suspend, screen lock and
547	  unlock, the systemd service (start, restart after `kill -9`, clean stop).
548	
549	## 10. Limitations and future work
550	
551	- **Keys, not text.** What an app does with a key is invisible: autocomplete,
552	  auto-closing brackets (except in VS Code with tier 2), IME conversion, tab
553	  completion and zsh autosuggestions in shells, Ctrl+R history search.
554	  Shell history recall only knows commands brain saw being run.
555	- **The mouse is not captured.** A click tells brain the cursor moved but not
556	  where in the text. Text edited after moving the cursor with the mouse
557	  (clicking into a line, mouse selection, drag and drop) is not supported:
558	  typing continues from where the keyboard last left the cursor. Switching
559	  *tabs* of one window with the mouse within 1 s of a keystroke would be
560	  taken as a title rename (another window being activated never is).
561	- **Held keys.** brain logs KDE's repeat schedule exactly, but each app runs
562	  its own repeat timer; Qt's may fire up to 5 % early or late, so a held key
563	  can produce one character more or less in the app than in brain.
564	- **Compose, dead keys, IME** are not interpreted; dead keys are logged by
565	  name.
566	- **Clock steps backwards** (NTP corrections, manual changes) break the
567	  "log in time order" assumption `query text` relies on: events in its window
568	  written after such a step can be missed. Both bounds can be made exact using
569	  the checkpoints' 5 s spacing (start at the earliest checkpoint within 5 s
570	  before the window, stop after the last one within 5 s after it); not done.
571	- **Other password prompts** are captured. AT-SPI's `password text` role
572	  would allow skipping them in apps that expose it.
573	- **VS Code tier 2** assumes the cursor starts at the end of the file,
574	  replays faster than a human (so accepting a suggestion may not replay the
575	  same), runs without extensions when they exceed 300 MB, and is the one part
576	  of `brain.db` a rebuild from the log does not reproduce (its file snapshot
577	  must be taken within 2 minutes of the session starting, before the file
578	  is saved).
579	- **Desktop scope**: focus tracking needs KWin. On GNOME the equivalent would
580	  be a Shell extension; on wlroots compositors, `wlr-foreign-toplevel`. Keys
581	  are captured on any Linux, attributed to `unknown`.
582	- **Future work**: AT-SPI as a second source for GTK/Qt apps; the
583	  sandboxed-replay approach of tier 2 for terminals (a pty with the user's
584	  shell) and Chrome (CDP with a companion extension); retention and
585	  compaction of old log data.

# PLAN — `brain`, a shadow assistant for Linux (KDE Plasma 6 / Wayland)

This is the research and architecture write-up for `brain`: how keystrokes
and application context are collected, how they are ingested, how writing
sessions are defined and their text reconstructed, how everything is stored
and indexed, and how queries read it. It describes the code as built; the
original design doc is in `ai-logs/design-doc.md`, and the places where the
build deliberately differs from it are called out ("Differs from the design").

## 1. Summary

```
 keyboards ──► input thread ──► Recorder ──► events.jsonl  (append-only, ground truth)
 (evdev,         │ xkbcommon      ▲ app + window                │ ~1 s
  passive)       │ key repeat     │ from KWin                   ▼
                 ▼                │                       ingest thread ──► brain.db (SQLite WAL)
 KWin script ──D-Bus──────────────┘                         │ sessions        sessions + FTS5 (trigram)
 Klipper (paste text), screen lock, sleep, layouts ─────────┘ reconstruction  context_state
                                                              checkpoints     log_checkpoints
                                    tier 2 worker (opt-in): VS Code replay ──┘
 brain query search ──► brain.db (read-only snapshot)
 brain query text   ──► log_checkpoints → events.jsonl
```

* **Capture** reads keyboards directly from the kernel (evdev), passively, and
  resolves each key to the character the app receives with libxkbcommon and
  the user's real layouts. Focus (app id and window title) comes from a KWin
  script calling back over D-Bus. Every event is one JSON line appended to
  `events.jsonl`.
* **Ingest** (a thread in the same process) tails the log about once a
  second. In one SQLite transaction per batch it writes log checkpoints,
  opens, updates and closes writing sessions, reconstructs their text, and
  advances the log offset. The log is the ground truth; the database is
  derived from it and can be rebuilt from it.
* **Query** reads the database (`search`) or the log (`text`) while `run`
  keeps writing, and prints JSON.
* **Threads in `brain run`**: main (signals, orderly shutdown), input (the
  hot path), ingest, one small thread per watched D-Bus signal plus zbus's
  own connection threads, and with `--vscode-replay` a tier 2 worker. A real
  run has 13 threads.
* **Measured cost**: 0.1 % CPU and 8 MB peak RSS while typing at human speed
  with queries running (`tests/perf_budget.rs`); the budget is 1 % and 32 MB.

## 2. Research: collecting keystrokes and application data

### 2.1 The constraint that shapes everything: Wayland

On X11, any client can read global input (XRecord, XInput2 raw events) and the
active window (`_NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW`). Wayland removed both on purpose. Clients
only receive input while they have focus, and there is no standard protocol
for asking "which window is active". Global capture therefore needs one of:
kernel-level input access, cooperation from the compositor, or cooperation from
each application. Every approach below falls into one of those three groups.

### 2.2 Keystrokes: approaches compared

| # | Approach | Works on KDE Wayland? | What it sees | Permissions | Latency / CPU | Text fidelity | Robustness | Invasiveness / risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | **evdev read** (`/dev/input/event*`, non-grabbing) | Yes, independent of the display server | Raw keycodes + press/release/repeat, kernel timestamps | `input` group (or a udev ACL) | No added latency (passive parallel reader); a few µs per event | Keys, not text. Characters need an xkb keymap that mirrors the compositor's | Must handle hotplug, `ENODEV` after resume, `SYN_DROPPED` | Read-only; but `input` group can read **every** keyboard, a real security cost |
| B | **libinput as a library** (path/udev backend over the same nodes) | Yes | Same keycodes, normalized; adds touchpad/gesture processing | Same as A (udev backend also wants seat access) | Slightly higher than A (more processing, larger dependency) | Same as A | Device handling done for us, but its udev backend assumes it owns the seat | Same as A; also pulls in libinput, libudev, libevdev |
| C | **X11 XRecord / XInput2 raw events** | XWayland clients only | Keycodes/keysyms via the X server | None on X11 | Low | Keysyms; native Wayland apps invisible | Fine on X11 | Not viable on Wayland: Konsole, Firefox (Wayland), most KDE apps are native |
| D | **Grab + forward proxy** (`EVIOCGRAB` + re-emit via `/dev/uinput`; keyd/kmonad style) | Yes | Same as A, exclusive | `input` + write access to `/dev/uinput` (root-only here) | **Adds a hop to every keystroke** (read → uinput → kernel → compositor) | Same as A | If the proxy hangs, the keyboard is dead; crashes release the grab but drop held keys | High: brain sits *in* the input path, and that hop is exactly what "no input lag" forbids |
| E | **Kernel module / eBPF** (input handler, kprobe on the input core, HID-BPF) | Yes | Keycodes (HID-BPF: HID reports) | root / `CAP_BPF`+`CAP_PERFMON`; module signing under Secure Boot | Very low | Same as A | Breaks across kernel versions (kprobes are not ABI); module crash = kernel crash | Very high. Needs root for an end-user tool, and looks like a rootkit |
| F | **AT-SPI accessibility bus** (`text-changed`, `text-caret-moved`, focus events) | Yes, where apps cooperate | **Actual widget text**, insertions and deletions, caret, role (can skip `password text` fields) | None (session bus) | Event volume is per text change; enabling a11y in Chromium/Electron has a noticeable cost | Best for GTK/Qt widgets; Chrome/Electron need `--force-renderer-accessibility`; terminals expose little or nothing; many apps expose nothing | Apps must be started with a11y on; Qt needs a11y enabled | Low privilege, but changes app behaviour (a11y trees) and coverage is uneven |
| G | **Input-method framework** (IBus engine / Fcitx5 addon; on KWin via `input-method-v1`) | Only in IM-aware clients | Key events routed to the IM, **committed text** (handles compose/IME correctly) | None, but it must *be* the user's IM | Low | Correct committed text, but no view of edits inside the widget (backspace into existing text, mouse selection) | Clients without text-input support (some terminals, XWayland, games) are invisible | Replaces the user's IM (conflicts with CJK users' setup); every keystroke now depends on brain |
| H | **Compositor hook** (KWin C++ effect/plugin, or patched KWin) | Yes | Keys after the compositor's own xkb processing + the exact focused surface | Install into KWin's plugin dir | Very low | Best key-level fidelity: same keymap, same repeat, same focus as apps actually get | KWin's C++ plugin API is not stable; must rebuild for every KWin release | A bug crashes the whole desktop session. KWin *scripts* (JS) have no key-event API |
| I | **LD_PRELOAD / toolkit hooks** (wrap `wl_keyboard` listeners, Qt/GTK input) | Partly | Whatever the hooked process receives | None | Low | Good per process | Flatpak/Snap sandboxes, static binaries, setuid and already-running apps are missed; breaks on toolkit updates | Injects code into every app |
| J | **Per-app extensions** (browser extension, VS Code extension, shell `PROMPT_COMMAND`/zsh hooks) | Yes | **The real document state** (`onDidChangeTextDocument`, DOM `input` events, the executed command line) | Per-app install | Low | Highest possible, but only inside that app | Each app's extension API | One integration per app; doesn't meet "follows what they write in each application" by itself |
| K | **xdg-desktop-portal** (GlobalShortcuts, InputCapture, RemoteDesktop/EIS) | n/a | GlobalShortcuts: only registered shortcuts. InputCapture: input only after the pointer crosses a barrier (made for Synergy-style sharing). RemoteDesktop: *sends* input | User consent dialog | — | None of them give a passive global key stream | — | Not usable, by design |

**Notes on the close calls:**

- **evdev (A) vs libinput (B).** Both read the same device nodes. libinput's
  value is pointer acceleration, touchpad gestures and tablet handling, none
  of which a key logger needs. Reading evdev directly keeps the dependency
  set and the memory footprint small, and gives full control over hotplug and
  resync.
- **Why not grab (D).** A passive reader is not on the input path: the kernel
  delivers each event to every open evdev client independently, so if brain
  stalls the user notices nothing. A grab-and-forward proxy makes every
  keystroke wait on brain and fails with a frozen keyboard.
- **AT-SPI (F)** is the only system-wide source that sees real text rather
  than keys. Coverage decides against it: Chrome/Electron, VS Code and
  terminals, the main targets, are its weak spots. It remains the best
  candidate for a second source that corrects key-based reconstruction for
  GTK/Qt apps (section 10).
- **Compositor hook (H)** has the best fidelity, but a C++ plugin loaded into
  KWin breaks with every KWin release and a bug takes the desktop down. brain
  takes the one thing it needs from the compositor (focus) through KWin's
  supported scripting interface, and mirrors its keymap and repeat settings
  instead of hooking it.

**Decision: evdev (A), passive and never grabbed, with characters resolved by
libxkbcommon.** (`src/capture/input.rs`, `keys.rs`, `xkb.rs`)

- **Devices.** Every `/dev/input/event*` whose key bitmap has A, Z, Space and
  Enter is a keyboard. Each gets an event-type mask (`EVIOCSMASK`: only
  `EV_SYN` and `EV_KEY`), so the kernel never wakes brain for LEDs, scan codes
  or anything else. Mice and touchpads are not opened at all (section 10:
  a click says the cursor moved, not where to).
- **Hotplug.** inotify on `/dev/input` (`IN_CREATE`, and `IN_ATTRIB` because
  udev applies the `input` group permissions after creating the node). A
  device that disappears releases its held keys, so a modifier can never get
  stuck.
- **One poll loop.** The input thread sleeps in `poll(2)` on the keyboards,
  the inotify fd and an eventfd for control messages, with a timeout only
  while a key is held (for repeat). Per keystroke: one `read`, an xkbcommon
  update, JSON into a reused buffer, one `write`.
- **Characters.** One keymap from the compositor's own layout settings, read
  in KWin's order: `kxkbrc` (when its layout list is in use), the
  `XKB_DEFAULT_*` environment of the session, then systemd-localed. One
  modifier state shared by all keyboards, as KWin keeps it (Shift on one
  keyboard plus a letter on another gives a capital). KDE's layout switches
  are followed two ways: Alt+Shift is applied by xkbcommon itself (the same
  `grp:` option the compositor uses), and `org.kde.KeyboardLayouts`
  `layoutChanged`/`layoutListChanged` signals set the layout when it is
  switched from the tray or the list changes.
- **Shortcuts on the Latin layout.** With Ctrl, Alt or Super held, a key that
  is not Latin in the active layout is resolved in the first layout where it
  is (Ctrl+ש is logged as Ctrl+A), because that is how Qt, GTK and Chromium
  match shortcuts. Plain typing stays in the active layout.
- **Key repeat.** On Wayland the kernel's repeat events are not what apps
  see: each app repeats keys itself on the schedule the compositor
  advertises. brain ignores kernel repeats (`value == 2`) and synthesizes
  repeats on KDE's schedule (`kcminputrc`, default 600 ms delay, 25 Hz), for
  keys that repeat in the keymap, cancelled by release or by a new press.
  Repeats are emitted in time order with the transitions around them: on
  every wakeup the loop first reads every queued key event, then emits the
  repeats due by the time it sampled before reading.
- **Timestamps.** The kernel's timestamp of each event is logged, not the
  time brain read it.
- **Resync.** On `SYN_DROPPED` the real key state is re-read
  (`EVIOCGKEY`) and held keys reconciled.

### 2.3 Application and focus data: approaches compared

| Approach | Works on KDE Wayland? | What it gives | Permissions | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **KWin script + D-Bus callback** (chosen) | Yes (and KWin X11) | Activation events, caption changes, `desktopFileName`, `resourceClass`, pid, for native Wayland *and* XWayland windows | None; loaded via KWin's own `org.kde.KWin /Scripting` interface | Event-driven, zero polling | Supported, stable JS API. The script runs inside the compositor but is sandboxed JS; a bug cannot crash KWin the way a C++ plugin can |
| `kdotool` | Yes | One-shot queries (active window, title) | None | Each call loads a temporary KWin script; polling would be expensive | Same mechanism, wrapped as a CLI. Good proof the approach is sound; unsuitable as an event source |
| `wlr-foreign-toplevel-management` | No (wlroots compositors: Sway, Hyprland, …) | Toplevel list + activated state | None | Event-driven | Not implemented by KWin. The newer `ext-foreign-toplevel-list-v1` deliberately carries **no** activation state, so it cannot answer "which window is focused" anyway |
| KDE `org_kde_plasma_window_management` | Only for privileged clients | Full window list + state (what the Plasma task manager uses) | KWin restricts it to trusted clients (desktop-file allowlisting) | Event-driven | Not meant for third-party tools; relies on KDE-internal trust configuration |
| X11 `_NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW` / `WM_CLASS` | XWayland only | Active *X* window | None | Event-driven (PropertyNotify) | Native Wayland windows are invisible to XWayland clients |
| AT-SPI focus events | Partly | Focused accessible object + its app | None | Event-driven | Same coverage problem as in 2.2; also gives no stable app id |
| GNOME Shell extension | GNOME only | Equivalent of the KWin script (`global.display` `notify::focus-window`) | Extension install | Event-driven | The GNOME port of our design; out of scope |
| `/proc` + compositor-agnostic heuristics | No | — | — | — | No way to know focus from process state |

**Decision: a KWin script that pushes focus changes into brain over D-Bus.**
(`src/capture/desktop.rs`, `kwin_focus.js`)

- `brain run` claims `org.shadowassistant.Brain.p<pid>` on the session bus
  and exports one method, `Activated(desktopFile, resourceClass, caption,
  renamed)`.
  It writes a small script and loads it through KWin's own
  `org.kde.KWin /Scripting` interface. The script reports
  `workspace.windowActivated` (`renamed = false`) and the active window's
  `captionChanged` (`renamed = true`), and the current window right away.
  Focus events in the log carry `"renamed": true` for title changes. Calls
  from anyone but KWin's bus name are ignored.
- The app id is the window's desktop file name (`org.kde.kate`,
  `google-chrome`, `com.microsoft.VSCode`), falling back to the X11
  resource class. Every key is stamped with the current app and window
  title, so each log line is self-describing.
- If KWin restarts (`NameOwnerChanged`), or is not up yet when brain starts
  as a service, the script is loaded as soon as KWin's name appears. A
  script left loaded by a `brain run` killed with -9 is unloaded by the next
  start.

**Screen lock.** `org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver` `ActiveChanged` (and
`GetActive` at start): while locked, keys are still read (to keep modifier
state right) but nothing is logged, so the unlock password never is. `lock`
and `unlock` are logged, and the focus is re-stated after unlock.

**Paste.** On Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Shift+V or Shift+Insert the clipboard is read from
Klipper (`getClipboardContents`, 300 ms timeout, up to 64 KiB) and logged as a
`paste` event right after the key. Copying alone is never recorded.

**Sleep/wake.** logind's `PrepareForSleep` on the system bus: `sleep` and
`wake` are logged, and on wake every keyboard is closed and reopened (held
keys released). Tested with a real suspend through `systemctl suspend`.

## 3. Event format and ingestion

### 3.1 The capture log

`events.jsonl`, one JSON object per line, in the assignment's format plus the
window title:

```json
{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:37:56.937Z","app":"org.kde.kate","type":"key","key":"H","mods":["shift"],"window":"notes.md — Kate"}
{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:37:57.132Z","app":"org.kde.kate","type":"key","key":"Backspace","mods":[],"repeat":true,"window":"notes.md — Kate"}
{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:38:00.003Z","app":"google-chrome","type":"focus","window":"New tab - Google Chrome"}
{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:38:01.120Z","app":"google-chrome","type":"focus","window":"brain - Google Search - Google Chrome","renamed":true}
{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:38:02.410Z","app":"google-chrome","type":"paste","text":"pasted words","window":"New tab - Google Chrome"}
{"ts":"2026-11-16T11:36:48.298Z","app":"org.kde.kate","type":"system","state":"sleep"}
```

Types: `key` (with `repeat: true` for synthesized repeats), `focus` (a
window activated, or with `renamed: true` the active window's title
changed), `paste`, and `system` (`start`, `stop`,
`sleep`, `wake`, `lock`, `unlock`). Timestamps are RFC 3339 UTC with
milliseconds: fixed width, so they sort as strings.

### 3.2 Write path

- One `write(2)` per event, of a complete line, from the input thread (or a
  D-Bus thread for focus, lock and sleep events) under one mutex. The event
  is in the kernel's page cache when the call returns, so a crash of brain
  loses nothing; a power loss can lose the last second.
- `fdatasync` at most once per second, from the ingest thread, only if
  something was written.
- On open, a torn last line (a `kill -9` or power loss mid-write) is cut off;
  readers only ever return complete lines.

### 3.3 Ingest

Once a second, the ingest thread syncs the log and runs steps of at most 5,000
lines until it has caught up. **Each step is one SQLite transaction** that
holds everything derived from those lines and the new log offset:

1. read complete lines from `ingest_state.log_offset`;
2. write a log checkpoint at most every 5 s of log time;
3. feed each event to the session engine (section 4);
4. once caught up, close sessions idle on the wall clock, write finished tier
   2 results, refresh the live text of open sessions;
5. store the new offset and commit.

If the commit fails nothing is visible and the same lines are read again; the
in-memory session state is rebuilt from the database first, so it cannot run
ahead. After the commit, tier 2 jobs are handed to the worker.

**Why a thread in the same process**: one binary and one lock on the data
directory, no IPC, and ingest can never run without capture or vice versa.
The capture path never touches SQLite, so a slow transaction cannot delay
reading the keyboard.

**Why not write keystrokes to SQLite directly**: a SQLite write can stall
(WAL checkpoints, FTS updates, lock contention), and a stalled reader of the
keyboard overflows the kernel's small buffer and loses keys. The append-only
log also makes the database disposable: a schema change, or a bug in session
logic, is fixed by deleting `brain.db`, which is rebuilt from the log.

### 3.4 `kill -9` at each point

| Killed while... | After restart |
|---|---|
| writing a log line | the torn line is cut off; everything before it is intact |
| between a write and the next ingest | ingest resumes from its offset and reads the new lines |
| inside an ingest transaction | SQLite rolls it back; the offset still points before those lines, so they are read again: no gap, no duplicate |
| with sessions open | open sessions are rebuilt from the database and their events replayed from the log (section 4.5); the restart's `start` event then closes them |

`tests/crash_safety.rs` kills brain 25 times under load and checks database
integrity, offsets on line boundaries, a complete log, and that every session,
document and checkpoint equals a clean rebuild from the log.

## 4. Sessions and reconstruction

(`src/sessions.rs`, `src/reconstruct/`)

### 4.1 Definition

- A session is one **`(app, window title)`**. The title is normalized first:
  leading status glyphs are removed (an editor's unsaved-file dot, the
  spinners terminal programs animate in titles) and so are `*` / `[modified]`
  markers, because they change while typing.
- **Titles renamed by the typing itself** keep the session: VS Code names a
  new file after its first line, a mail window after its subject. A title
  change *of the same window* (a `renamed` focus event) within 1 s of a
  keystroke in it, with no shortcut in between (Ctrl+Tab, Alt+Tab may switch
  tabs or windows), makes the new title an alias of the open session. A
  window activation, by keyboard or mouse, ends any possible rename.
- A session **closes** after **30 s without activity in that window**, or at
  once when a single-line field commits (Enter at a shell prompt, in a chat
  box, an address bar or a launcher), is cancelled (Ctrl+C at a prompt), or
  is left for another field of the same window (Tab, Ctrl+L/K/T/W in a
  browser), and when `brain run` stops or restarts.
- **Focus loss alone never closes a session**: switching away and back
  within 30 s of that window's last keystroke resumes it.
- Shortcuts with no modelled effect (Ctrl+C copy, Alt+Tab, Ctrl+S, F-keys)
  are not activity: they neither open nor extend a session.
- A session that changed nothing (cursor movement only, a typo typed and
  deleted, whitespace) leaves no row; a committed non-empty line always
  does (a shell command run again from history).
- **Idle closing on the clock** happens only once ingest has caught up with
  the log, and 2 s past the 30 s timeout, so it always agrees with the same
  rule applied to event times on a rebuild.

### 4.2 Text across sessions

Editors and unknown (multi-line) apps keep a **document per window** between
sessions (`context_state`, forgotten after 24 h), so the next session
continues where the previous one left it, cursor included. A session's text
is that document when the session closes: a word present at close stays
findable through that session even if a later session deletes it.
Single-line fields (terminals, browsers, chat, launchers) start every session
empty: their titles are reused by unrelated fields ("New tab", "~"), so
carrying text over would mix them.

### 4.3 The engine: incremental, in memory, from the log

Ingest keeps one entry per open session in memory: its row id, a text buffer
(the reconstruction so far, with cursor, selection and undo history), and its
last activity. Each logged event is routed by its own `(app, window)` to its
session and applied once, the moment ingest reads it; switching between apps
is just a different map entry. The log interleaves apps, but filtering it per
key preserves each window's order. Every ingest step writes the current text
of changed open sessions, so `search` sees what is being typed now. Closing a
session writes the text it already has.

*Differs from the design*, which reconstructed each session at close and
rebuilt open sessions just in time for live search. The result is the same;
incremental work costs a constant amount per key instead of growing with the
session.

### 4.4 Reconstruction tiers

- **Tier 0, a generic text field** (`reconstruct/buffer.rs`): insertion
  replacing the selection, Backspace/Delete (word-wise with Ctrl), arrows,
  Home/End, Up/Down keeping the column, PageUp/PageDown, Shift-selection,
  select-all, cut, and undo/redo grouped about a word at a time. A 200,000
  character cap per buffer keeps memory bounded. An unknown cursor position
  is assumed to be at the end.
- **Tier 1, per-app rules** (`reconstruct/apps.rs`, `editor.rs`): a small
  table classifies app ids into terminal, browser, chat, launcher, editor or
  generic. It decides whether Enter commits or inserts a newline (Shift+Enter
  is a newline in browsers and chat), readline editing in terminals
  (Ctrl+A/E/U/K/W, Alt+B/F) and history recall with Up/Down from the commands
  brain saw committed in that terminal app, browser field changes, and that
  plain Ctrl+V does not paste in a terminal.
- **Tier 2, VS Code replayed in VS Code** (`reconstruct/vscode/`,
  `tier2.rs`, opt-in with `--vscode-replay`): when a VS Code session opens,
  the file is identified from the window title: an absolute path if the
  title has one, otherwise the title's file name looked up in VS Code's
  per-workspace state for the window's folder (its open editors, which also
  covers files opened from outside the folder), under that folder, then in
  the window's editor history; one existing match is required. VS Code
  writes that state with a delay, so an unidentified file is looked up
  again on each ingest step while the session is open, for up to 2 minutes.
  The file is copied, unless it is an unsaved new file (`Untitled-1`), had
  unsaved changes when the session started, or changed on disk after the
  session started (a late snapshot is therefore still the starting text).
  When the session closes with its tier 0/1 text, a worker works out its
  real text. If the file on disk was written after the session's last
  keystroke (autosave, or Ctrl+S at the end), it already holds what VS Code
  made of the keys: the session's text is a git-style unified diff from the
  snapshot to the saved file, 3 lines of context (`done: saved file`,
  exact, VS Code not started; Myers line diff with git's "slide down"
  placement of ambiguous runs). Otherwise the
  worker replays the session's own keystrokes from the log into one warm,
  headless VS Code (Electron's headless mode, no display server) over the
  DevTools protocol on a pipe, in its own network namespace and a
  CPU/memory-capped systemd scope, with the user's settings and keybindings,
  saves, and takes the changed lines (`done: replayed (best effort,
  unverified)`: cursor assumed at the end, no extensions above 300 MB, so
  extension autocomplete is not reproduced). Failures and timeouts keep the
  tier 0/1 text; pending jobs survive restarts.

  With tier 2 on, every VS Code key except desktop (Super) shortcuts opens
  or extends the session, even ones tier 0/1 ignores (Ctrl+D, Alt+Up,
  Ctrl+S), and a session with a snapshot is kept at close even if its tier
  0/1 text is unchanged (`pending: saved file only`): it gets the saved
  file's diff, or is removed when the file was not saved after it; any
  session whose saved diff is empty is removed too. Because the snapshot is
  taken when ingest opens the session (up to 1 s after the first key), a
  focus change to VS Code wakes the ingest thread at once and the file is
  copied on focus; a session that starts within 10 s and finds its file
  saved before its own snapshot uses that copy, if the file was not
  modified after the session started.

*Differs from the design*: no Xvfb (headless Electron needs no display), and
the CDP connection is a pipe, because the network namespace makes a TCP port
unreachable.

### 4.5 Restart with open sessions

On start, ingest loads the sessions still open in the database, restores
their starting documents from `context_state`, and replays their events from
each session's `start_offset` up to the ingested offset, through the same
key-to-action rules. The `start` event that follows closes them (input while
brain was not running is unknown). Everything the engine decides is a
function of the log, so a database rebuilt from the log alone is identical;
`sessions::tests::crash_recovery_reproduces_an_uninterrupted_run` restarts
ingest after every line to prove it.

## 5. Storage and indexing

### 5.1 Layout

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `events.jsonl` | the capture log (0600), ground truth |
| `brain.db` (+ `-wal`, `-shm`) | SQLite index, derived |
| `run.lock` | flock held by the running `brain run` |
| `kwin/` | the generated KWin script |
| `vscode/` | tier 2 sandbox and file snapshots |

The directory is created 0700 and brain runs with umask 077.

### 5.2 Schema (version 4)

- **`sessions`**: `id`, `app`, `window` (normalized), `started_at`,
  `ended_at` (NULL while open), `status`, `tier_used`, `reconstructed_text`,
  `start_offset` / `end_offset` (the session's events in the log),
  `end_reason` (`idle`, `commit`, `cancel`, `field`, `stop`, `restart`),
  `tier2_status`, `tier2_file`. Indexes on `(app, started_at)`, `status`, and
  `(app, end_reason, end_offset)` for shell history.
- **`sessions_fts`**: FTS5 over `reconstructed_text`, external content (the
  text is stored once, in `sessions`), kept in sync by insert/update/delete
  triggers in the same transaction.
- **`context_state`**: each multi-line window's document between sessions.
- **`ingest_state`**: the single log offset.
- **`log_checkpoints`**: `(ts, byte_offset)`, at most one per 5 s of log time.

There are no migrations (first version): a database from another schema
version is refused with a message to delete it.

### 5.3 Why SQLite, WAL and FTS5

- **WAL**: one writer (ingest) never blocks readers, and each `brain query`
  sees a snapshot as of the start of its read: never a half-written session.
- **`synchronous = NORMAL`**: no fsync per commit. A power loss can drop the
  last commits but never corrupts the database, and the dropped work is
  re-derived from the log because the offset rolls back with it.
- **FTS5** is in SQLite itself (bundled, no server), and external content
  avoids storing session text twice.
- A 1 MiB page cache keeps the writer inside the memory budget.

### 5.4 Tokenizer: trigram

The index uses FTS5's **trigram** tokenizer, case- and accent-insensitive: a
query word matches anywhere inside a word (`run` finds "rerun", `cafe` finds
"Café"). *Differs from the design* (porter stemming), on the owner's call:
search should behave as "contains", and porter is English-only, while
trigram finds Hebrew words with attached prefixes (`בית` in "בבית"). Words
shorter than 3 characters cannot use the trigram index and are matched with
`LIKE`.

### 5.5 Log checkpoints

`query text` must read the keys of a time window from the log without
scanning it from the start. Each checkpoint says "the event at this byte has
this timestamp". Because the log is written in time order, starting at the
latest checkpoint at or before the window misses nothing, and reads at most
5 s of log before the window; reading stops 60 s of log after it. Per-app
checkpoints would not save work, since the log interleaves apps and the
window has to be read anyway. Clock steps backwards are discussed in section
10.

## 6. Query semantics

(`src/query.rs`)

- **`brain query search "<words>" [--app A] [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]
  [--limit N]`**: sessions whose text contains every word (substrings, any
  case), newest first, default limit 20, with a snippet around the first
  match. Open sessions are included with their live text and
  `ended_at: null`. A session is in a time window if it overlaps it.
- **`brain query text --app A [--from T] [--to T] [--at T]`**: what was typed
  into the app during the time range, reconstructed. The range's key and
  paste events (read from the log, section 5.5) are split per app window
  (window title) and each app window's events run, from an empty text,
  through the app's tier 0/1 adapter: the same `editor::action` and
  `FieldEditor` the session engine uses, without sessions. A submit in a
  single-line field (Enter at a shell prompt) keeps the line and continues
  on a fresh one; Up recalls lines submitted earlier in the same app window.
  Output: `windows` (each app window's text, by first keystroke) and `text`
  (them joined, one per line). *Differs from the design*, where `text` was
  the raw keystroke stream; the owner changed it.
- **`--app A`** can be part of an app id, ignoring case. `search` keeps
  every matching app; `text` resolves it to one full id (exact match first,
  else the single id containing it; ambiguous or unknown is an error) and
  reports that id.
- **Windows**: `--at T` is the 10 minutes ending at T; `--from` alone runs to
  now; `--from` and `--to` together are explicit; `--to` alone is the 10
  minutes ending at T for `text` and everything up to T for `search`; no
  flags means the last 10 minutes for `text` and all time for `search`.
- **Times**: relative (`-30s`, `-15m`, `-2h`, `-1d`, `-1h30m`, `now`), local
  (`2026-11-16 14:00`, a date, or a time of day meaning today; DST folds
  take the earlier instant, DST gaps are an error), or RFC 3339 with a zone.
  Output times are local with their offset (RFC 3339), and the resolved
  window is echoed; the log and the database store UTC.
- Errors (empty query, bad time, empty window, `--at` with `--from`/`--to`,
  missing data directory) go to stderr with a non-zero exit code.

## 7. Resource budget

- **No input lag by construction**: brain is a passive reader, not on the
  delivery path. Even a completely stalled brain cannot delay a keystroke.
- **CPU**: no async runtime and no polling. The input thread sleeps in
  `poll` and wakes per key event (and per repeat while a key is held); one
  `write` per event; one small transaction per second; SQLite work per
  session proportional to its text.
- **Memory**: few threads with small stacks, a 1 MiB SQLite cache, a capped
  buffer per open session (usually one to three are open), no copy of closed
  sessions in memory.
- **Measured** (`tests/perf_budget.rs`, part of `cargo test`): 8 keys/s for
  30 s through the whole pipeline with a query every 3 s: **0.1 % CPU, 8.1 MB
  peak RSS**. A real run idles at about 8 MB.
- The opt-in VS Code instance runs outside brain's budget, in its own
  systemd scope capped at 50 % CPU and 1.5 GB, shut down after 10 minutes
  idle.

## 8. Security and privacy

- **Local only.** No network code in brain; the VS Code replay instance runs
  in a network namespace with only loopback.
- **Data at rest**: directory 0700, files 0600.
- **Privilege**: brain runs as the user, as a systemd *user* service if
  wanted (`make install-service`), never as root. The service's data is its
  systemd state directory (`~/.local/state/brain`, mode 0700), deleted by
  `make uninstall-service` unless `KEEP_DATA=1`. Reading keyboards needs
  the `input` group, which lets any process of the user read all keyboards;
  the README states this trade-off.
- **Passwords**: capture pauses while the screen is locked. Other password
  prompts (sudo in a terminal, web logins) cannot be told apart from typing
  by key events alone (section 10).
- **Clipboard**: read only on a paste shortcut.
- **KWin integration** only reads window metadata and calls one D-Bus
  method; calls not coming from KWin are ignored.
- **Queries**: search words are quoted for FTS5 and all SQL uses bound
  parameters.
- **Tests that need privileges** get exactly two narrow ones
  (`scripts/setup-test-permissions.sh`): passwordless `rtcwake -m no -s 30`
  only, and `/dev/uinput` for the user at the local seat.

## 9. Testing strategy

- **Unit tests** (about 120, `cargo test`): key resolution and layouts,
  repeat synthesis (including a 300-scenario stress test against an
  independent model, with random early and late wakeups), the recorder, the
  log's torn-tail repair, schema and search, ingest, the tier 0 buffer and
  tier 1 rules, title normalization and renames, every session rule, crash
  recovery after every line, time parsing, query windows, and `query text`'s
  per-window reconstruction (the README's example, event for event).
- **Integration tests run by default**: `crash_safety` (25 `kill -9`s under
  load, compared with a clean rebuild), `query_cli` (the binary's JSON
  output, search semantics through the CLI, time windows, reconstructed
  text including the README's example, errors, and thousands of queries
  while `run` writes), `perf_budget` (CPU and
  memory budget).
- **Opt-in tests against real software**: `repeat_e2e` and
  `real_keyboard_e2e` type through a uinput keyboard into real Kate windows
  and compare Kate's saved files with brain (held-key repeats, Hebrew via
  Alt+Shift, focus moving between windows, keyboard unplug/replug);
  `vscode_replay` and `tier2_e2e` drive real VS Code.
- **Manual, once**: sleep/wake through a real suspend, screen lock and
  unlock, the systemd service (start, restart after `kill -9`, clean stop).

## 10. Limitations and future work

- **Keys, not text.** What an app does with a key is invisible: autocomplete,
  auto-closing brackets (except in VS Code with tier 2), IME conversion, tab
  completion and zsh autosuggestions in shells, Ctrl+R history search.
  Shell history recall only knows commands brain saw being run.
- **The mouse is not captured.** A click tells brain the cursor moved but not
  where in the text. Text edited after moving the cursor with the mouse
  (clicking into a line, mouse selection, drag and drop) is not supported:
  typing continues from where the keyboard last left the cursor. Switching
  *tabs* of one window with the mouse within 1 s of a keystroke would be
  taken as a title rename (another window being activated never is).
- **Held keys.** brain logs KDE's repeat schedule exactly, but each app runs
  its own repeat timer; Qt's may fire up to 5 % early or late, so a held key
  can produce one character more or less in the app than in brain.
- **Compose, dead keys, IME** are not interpreted; dead keys are logged by
  name.
- **Clock steps backwards** (NTP corrections, manual changes) break the
  "log in time order" assumption `query text` relies on: events in its window
  written after such a step can be missed. Both bounds can be made exact using
  the checkpoints' 5 s spacing (start at the earliest checkpoint within 5 s
  before the window, stop after the last one within 5 s after it); not done.
- **Other password prompts** are captured. AT-SPI's `password text` role
  would allow skipping them in apps that expose it.
- **VS Code tier 2** assumes the cursor starts at the end of the file,
  replays faster than a human (so accepting a suggestion may not replay the
  same), runs without extensions when they exceed 300 MB, and is the one part
  of `brain.db` a rebuild from the log does not reproduce (its file snapshot
  must be taken within 2 minutes of the session starting, before the file
  is saved).
- **Desktop scope**: focus tracking needs KWin. On GNOME the equivalent would
  be a Shell extension; on wlroots compositors, `wlr-foreign-toplevel`. Keys
  are captured on any Linux, attributed to `unknown`.
- **Future work**: AT-SPI as a second source for GTK/Qt apps; the
  sandboxed-replay approach of tier 2 for terminals (a pty with the user's
  shell) and Chrome (CDP with a companion extension); retention and
  compaction of old log data.

# CLAUDE.md — instructions for coding agents working on `brain`

`brain` is a Rust CLI for the Endpoint "Shadow Assistant" home assignment
(`Endpoint Home Assignment.pdf`, not committed). One binary, two commands:
`brain run` captures keystrokes + focus and stores them; `brain query`
(`search`, `text`) answers questions while `run` keeps going.

Design doc (source of truth for architecture):
https://claude.ai/artifact/UTxCHmXHeSBaQASSNNiSP9 — `PLAN.md` is the in-repo
research/architecture write-up and must stay consistent with the code.

## Target platform

Ubuntu, **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Not GNOME. Keys come from evdev
(`/dev/input/event*`, user in the `input` group), resolved with libxkbcommon
(`libxkbcommon.so.0`, linked by file name, so no `-dev` package is needed).
Focus comes from a KWin script calling back over D-Bus. Tests that run by
default must not need hardware, a desktop or privileges: use
`brain run --synthetic RATE` (hidden flag) to drive the real pipeline. Only
the opt-in (`#[ignore]`) tests use `/dev/uinput`, Kate or VS Code.

## Hard requirements (from the assignment) — never regress these

- Capture is invisible: no input lag (we never grab devices), **≤ 1 % average
  CPU while typing, ≤ 32 MB RSS**, keeps working after sleep/wake.
- `kill -9` of `run` at any moment + restart ⇒ no corruption
  (`tests/crash_safety.rs` must stay green).
- `query` works while `run` writes and always sees a consistent state.
- Both commands take `--data-dir` (default `./brain-data`) and exit non-zero
  with a message on stderr on error. Query output is JSON on stdout, with
  times in local time (the log and database store UTC).

## Decisions already made by the owner — do not re-litigate

- `brain query text` reconstructs "stupidly": the keys typed in the time
  range, per app and window title, run through the tier 0/1 adapters from
  an empty text (no sessions involved); output `windows` + joined `text`.
  It replaced the earlier raw-keystroke output at the owner's request.
  Range: default last 10 min, `--at T` = the 10 minutes ending at T, or
  `--from/--to`. Times accept relative (`-2h`), local and RFC 3339 forms.
  `--app` may be part of the id; `text` resolves it to exactly one app and
  reports the full id.
- Sessions: keyed by (app, normalized window title); close after 30 s idle
  in that context or on Enter in single-line contexts; focus loss alone
  never closes a session; a title change of the typed window (a `renamed`
  focus event) shortly after a keystroke keeps the session. With
  `--vscode-replay`, every VS Code key (not only text edits) opens or
  extends a session, and a session of shortcuts only (Ctrl+D, Ctrl+S) is
  kept for the saved file's diff, or removed when there is none.
- The mouse is not captured (owner's call): cursor moves made with the mouse
  are a documented limitation, not something to work around.
- Reconstruction tiers: 0 = generic buffer replay, 1 = per-app rules,
  2 = VS Code real-app replay, **opt-in** via `brain run --vscode-replay`,
  falling back to tier 0. Sessions, reconstruction and indexing are built
  before `brain query` (owner's call, changing the original stage order).
- Search is substring matching (FTS5 trigram, case- and accent-insensitive),
  not the design's porter stemming: `run` must find "rerun", `בית` "בבית".
- Sessions and their text must stay a pure function of the log: the crash
  test compares the live index with a fresh rebuild.
- Work went through stages (capture with sessions and indexing, query,
  end-to-end verification), each approved by the owner. Keep the habit for
  new work: build, run, test it yourself, report, then **stop and wait for
  explicit approval** before starting the next piece.

## Code map

```
src/main.rs              CLI (clap), error → stderr + exit 1
src/capture/mod.rs       `run` orchestration: sources, ingest thread, signals
src/capture/input.rs     poll loop over keyboards (evdev), hotplug, EVIOCSMASK
src/capture/keys.rs      pure key processing: xkb resolution + repeat synthesis
src/capture/xkb.rs       libxkbcommon FFI wrapper
src/capture/recorder.rs  stamps focus, appends to log, clipboard on paste, lock pause
src/capture/desktop.rs   D-Bus: KWin focus script, Klipper, lock, sleep, layouts
src/capture/synthetic.rs synthetic input source for tests/benchmarks
src/eventlog.rs          append-only JSONL log: torn-tail repair, line reader
src/store.rs             SQLite schema (WAL, FTS5), helpers
src/ingest.rs            log → SQLite, offset advanced in the same transaction
src/sessions.rs          session rules, open/close, live text, crash recovery
src/query.rs             `query search` / `query text`, time windows, JSON output
src/reconstruct/         buffer.rs tier 0 · apps.rs + editor.rs tier 1 ·
                         tier2.rs + vscode/ tier 2 (VS Code replay, opt-in)
src/event.rs, timefmt.rs event format, timestamp parsing/formatting
tests/                   integration tests that drive the real binary;
                         tests/common: uinput keyboard and KDE helpers
```

## Working rules

- **No backward compatibility.** This is the first robust version, still
  being built: change the log format, the schema or the CLI freely, with no
  migration, compatibility shims or legacy-format handling. Test data
  directories can be deleted and recreated.
- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` (zero warnings) and `cargo test`
  before every commit. Run `cargo test --release --test crash_safety` when
  touching the log, ingest or store.
- Keep the hot path (input thread) free of allocation-heavy work, blocking
  I/O other than the single log `write(2)`, and SQLite.
- The log is the ground truth; SQLite is derived and rebuildable. Never put
  data only in SQLite.
- Commit messages per https://cbea.ms/git-commit/ (imperative subject
  ≤ 50 chars, blank line, body wrapped at 72 explaining what and why).
  Commit at meaningful checkpoints.
- Prefer verifying behaviour by running the binary over reasoning about it;
  report exactly what was tested and what was not.
- Tests that need VS Code are `#[ignore]`: `cargo test --release --test
  vscode_replay --test tier2_e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1`.
- Every `brain run` a test starts goes through `tests/common::spawn_brain`
  (or `start_brain`): the guard stops it even when the test fails, and
  tests end with `assert_no_brain_on(data)`. No test may leave a process or
  a file behind.
- `tests/repeat_e2e.rs` and `tests/real_keyboard_e2e.rs` (`#[ignore]`) type
  into real Kate windows through /dev/uinput: they need an unlocked KDE
  session, `scripts/setup-test-permissions.sh`, and nobody touching the
  keyboard or mouse while they run. They only type while brain's log shows
  the intended window focused.
- The input loop must deliver key transitions before emitting the repeats
  due at the same time (`keys::tests::ticking_past_an_unread_release_adds_repeats`).
- Never change desktop session state you did not set up (lock/unlock,
  suspend); check it first and restore it.

https://claude.ai/artifact/UTxCHmXHeSBaQASSNNiSP9 — `PLAN.md` is the in-repo
research/architecture write-up and must stay consistent with the code.

## Target platform

Ubuntu, **KDE Plasma 6 on Wayland** (KWin). Not GNOME. Keys come from evdev
(`/dev/input/event*`, user in the `input` group), resolved with libxkbcommon
(`libxkbcommon.so.0`, linked by file name, so no `-dev` package is needed).
Focus comes from a KWin script calling back over D-Bus. Tests that run by
default must not need hardware, a desktop or privileges: use
`brain run --synthetic RATE` (hidden flag) to drive the real pipeline. Only
the opt-in (`#[ignore]`) tests use `/dev/uinput`, Kate or VS Code.

## Hard requirements (from the assignment) — never regress these

- Capture is invisible: no input lag (we never grab devices), **≤ 1 % average
  CPU while typing, ≤ 32 MB RSS**, keeps working after sleep/wake.
- `kill -9` of `run` at any moment + restart ⇒ no corruption
  (`tests/crash_safety.rs` must stay green).
- `query` works while `run` writes and always sees a consistent state.
- Both commands take `--data-dir` (default `./brain-data`) and exit non-zero
  with a message on stderr on error. Query output is JSON on stdout, with
  times in local time (the log and database store UTC).

## Decisions already made by the owner — do not re-litigate

- `brain query text` reconstructs "stupidly": the keys typed in the time
  range, per app and window title, run through the tier 0/1 adapters from
  an empty text (no sessions involved); output `windows` + joined `text`.
  It replaced the earlier raw-keystroke output at the owner's request.
  Range: default last 10 min, `--at T` = the 10 minutes ending at T, or
  `--from/--to`. Times accept relative (`-2h`), local and RFC 3339 forms.
  `--app` may be part of the id; `text` resolves it to exactly one app and
  reports the full id.
- Sessions: keyed by (app, normalized window title); close after 30 s idle
  in that context or on Enter in single-line contexts; focus loss alone
  never closes a session; a title change of the typed window (a `renamed`
  focus event) shortly after a keystroke keeps the session. With
  `--vscode-replay`, every VS Code key (not only text edits) opens or
  extends a session, and a session of shortcuts only (Ctrl+D, Ctrl+S) is
  kept for the saved file's diff, or removed when there is none.
- The mouse is not captured (owner's call): cursor moves made with the mouse
  are a documented limitation, not something to work around.
- Reconstruction tiers: 0 = generic buffer replay, 1 = per-app rules,
  2 = VS Code real-app replay, **opt-in** via `brain run --vscode-replay`,
  falling back to tier 0. Sessions, reconstruction and indexing are built
  before `brain query` (owner's call, changing the original stage order).
- Search is substring matching (FTS5 trigram, case- and accent-insensitive),
  not the design's porter stemming: `run` must find "rerun", `בית` "בבית".
- Sessions and their text must stay a pure function of the log: the crash
  test compares the live index with a fresh rebuild.
- Work went through stages (capture with sessions and indexing, query,
  end-to-end verification), each approved by the owner. Keep the habit for
  new work: build, run, test it yourself, report, then **stop and wait for
  explicit approval** before starting the next piece.

## Code map

```
src/main.rs              CLI (clap), error → stderr + exit 1
src/capture/mod.rs       `run` orchestration: sources, ingest thread, signals
src/capture/input.rs     poll loop over keyboards (evdev), hotplug, EVIOCSMASK
src/capture/keys.rs      pure key processing: xkb resolution + repeat synthesis
src/capture/xkb.rs       libxkbcommon FFI wrapper
src/capture/recorder.rs  stamps focus, appends to log, clipboard on paste, lock pause
src/capture/desktop.rs   D-Bus: KWin focus script, Klipper, lock, sleep, layouts
src/capture/synthetic.rs synthetic input source for tests/benchmarks
src/eventlog.rs          append-only JSONL log: torn-tail repair, line reader
src/store.rs             SQLite schema (WAL, FTS5), helpers
src/ingest.rs            log → SQLite, offset advanced in the same transaction
src/sessions.rs          session rules, open/close, live text, crash recovery
src/query.rs             `query search` / `query text`, time windows, JSON output
src/reconstruct/         buffer.rs tier 0 · apps.rs + editor.rs tier 1 ·
                         tier2.rs + vscode/ tier 2 (VS Code replay, opt-in)
src/event.rs, timefmt.rs event format, timestamp parsing/formatting
tests/                   integration tests that drive the real binary;
                         tests/common: uinput keyboard and KDE helpers
```

## Working rules

- **No backward compatibility.** This is the first robust version, still
  being built: change the log format, the schema or the CLI freely, with no
  migration, compatibility shims or legacy-format handling. Test data
  directories can be deleted and recreated.
- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` (zero warnings) and `cargo test`
  before every commit. Run `cargo test --release --test crash_safety` when
  touching the log, ingest or store.
- Keep the hot path (input thread) free of allocation-heavy work, blocking
  I/O other than the single log `write(2)`, and SQLite.
- The log is the ground truth; SQLite is derived and rebuildable. Never put
  data only in SQLite.
- Commit messages per https://cbea.ms/git-commit/ (imperative subject
  ≤ 50 chars, blank line, body wrapped at 72 explaining what and why).
  Commit at meaningful checkpoints.
- Prefer verifying behaviour by running the binary over reasoning about it;
  report exactly what was tested and what was not.
- Tests that need VS Code are `#[ignore]`: `cargo test --release --test
  vscode_replay --test tier2_e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1`.
- Every `brain run` a test starts goes through `tests/common::spawn_brain`
  (or `start_brain`): the guard stops it even when the test fails, and
  tests end with `assert_no_brain_on(data)`. No test may leave a process or
  a file behind.
- `tests/repeat_e2e.rs` and `tests/real_keyboard_e2e.rs` (`#[ignore]`) type
  into real Kate windows through /dev/uinput: they need an unlocked KDE
  session, `scripts/setup-test-permissions.sh`, and nobody touching the
  keyboard or mouse while they run. They only type while brain's log shows
  the intended window focused.
- The input loop must deliver key transitions before emitting the repeats
  due at the same time (`keys::tests::ticking_past_an_unread_release_adds_repeats`).
- Never change desktop session state you did not set up (lock/unlock,
  suspend); check it first and restore it.
